abstract: Geochronological analyses of samples of the Willochra Subgroup and the Tapley Hill Formation, which unconformably overlie the Beda Volcanics, give ages of 724±40 Ma and 750±53 Ma respectively, thereby indicating that the original age determination of 700 Ma for the Beda Volcanics is too young. New results suggest an age as old as 1075 Ma for the Beda Volcanics.  If the correlation with the Wooltana Volcanics in the Adelaide Geosyncline is correct, Willouran sedimentation must have occurred before 1075 Ma B.P.: so the break between the Callanna Beds and Burra Group sedimentation is thus of significant duration, since the Burra Group, near Adelaide, overlies a metamorphosed basement about 850 Ma old. The dates as now determined on the above two sedimentary units also place limits on the age of the Sturtian-Marinoan boundary.

abstract: An experimental Time Domain Induced Polarization (I.P.) Survey was carried out over the Olympic Dam copper deposit in order to establish instrument parameters necessary to detect the mineralisation. Cycle times of two and four seconds with a duty ratio of unity were used with varying delay times (td), and basic integrating periods (tp). The decay curve compiled from these data was used to ,select a cycle time of four seconds, a duty ratio of unity, a td of 1 440 ms and atp of 120 ms for production runs along two lines. These production runs failed to detect the mineralisation and it is suggested that this was due to lack of polarization of the ore body. Possible solutions to this problem are recommended. A Schlumberger vertical electrical sounding was carried out and a theoretical model fitted to the results. A deviation of field and model results at the deepest sounding values cannot be explained and further soundings are recommended.

title: RB 2014/00006 Geology of the Cultana 1:100 000 map sheet (6432).
notes:

Geographic Locality: North-eastern Eyre Peninsula;Northern Spencer Gulf;South-western Flinders Ranges;Cultana Army Training Area;Whyalla Conservation Park;Winninowie Conservation Park;Baroota Plain;Douglas Hills;Simmens Plateau;Long Sleep Plain;North Whyalla Hills;Mount Laura;Myall Creek;Tregalana Homestead;Backy Point;Wild Dog Hill;Douglas Point;Solution Hill;Nectar Brook;Mambray Creek;Spear Creek;Old Woolundunga Creek;Catninga Creek;Mount Gullet Creek;Pichi Richi Pass;Waukarie Creek;Two Hummock Point;White Cliff Dam;Point Lowly;The Sisters;El Alamein kimberlite sills;Fitzgerald Bay;Redcliff Point;Tent Hill;Bald Hill;Yatala Harbour;Cultana Fault;Point Paterson;Saltia Creek

Drillhole: Australian Selection PTR3/SAT1;(148490);PSH1/SAS1;(136943);PUB14/SAU4;(24921);PUB11/SAU3;(24891);Dampier Mining Co. UB6;(139420);UB16;(139881);SADME RED52;(24888);RED41;(24877);SG170;(24786);SG223;(24009);Australian Selection PUB45/SAU20;(139449)
abstract: The revised digital geology map of the Cultana 1:100 000 map sheet and accompanying geological descriptions in this report are the first components of the 2nd edition PORT AUGUSTA 1:250 000 map sheet to be completed. The subject map sheet occupies the north-eastern Eyre Peninsula, northern Spencer Gulf and south-western Flinders Ranges, and is underlain by rocks of the Mesoarchaean-Mesoproterozoic Gawler Craton, the Neoproterozoic Adelaide Geosyncline, Torrens Hinge Zone and Stuart Shelf, and the Tertiary Pirie Basin. The geological history of the area spans the Palaeoproterozoic to Quaternary, commencing with the deposition of sandstone of the Moonabie Formation at ~1755 Ma, which was subsequently deformed by open NW-trending folds, most probably during the Kararan Orogeny (1590–1555 Ma). This unit was intruded by Hiltaba Suite granites, including the Cultana Subsuite, and at the same time was overlain by felsic lavas of the Gawler Range Volcanics during the early Mesoproterozoic (~1590 Ma); this pervasive igneous activity occurred in response to regional  lithospheric extension and extensive intracrustal melting. The Hiltaba-GRV event was followed by deposition of fluvial sediments of the Pandurra Formation in the Cariewerloo Basin (maximum depositional age 1575 Ma, and possibly <1424 Ma). There is no subsequent geological rock record preserved on Cultana until the Neoproterozoic, when deposition of a thick succession of coastal to marine sediments and lesser mafic volcanics occurred within a rift basin in the Adelaide Geosyncline and Stuart Shelf. The initial phase of sedimentation and mafic magmatism occurred during the Willouran, comprising subaerial tholeiitic lava flows of the Beda Basalt, interlayered with fluvial sandstone of the Backy Point Formation, both overlying the easternmost Gawler Craton and Cariewerloo Basin on the Stuart Shelf. These units are contemporaneous with the Gairdner Dolerite dykes (~830 Ma), which intrude the Moonabie Formation, Cultana Subsuite and overlying Pandurra Formation on the Gawler Craton. During the late Sturtian, following the Sturtian glacial maximum, the Tapley Hill Formation and Brighton Limestone, units of a major transgressive/regressive sequence consisting of calcareous siltstone and limestone, were deposited in a shallowing marine basin extending throughout the Adelaide Geosyncline and Stuart Shelf. This was followed in the early Marinoan by deposition of two further transgressive/regressive sequences, the Angepena and Wilmington Formations, in tidal flat to shallow marine environments. During the later Marinoan, deposition resumed when fluvioglacial and deltaic sediments of the Elatina Formation were deposited in the Adelaide Geosyncline, contemporaneous with periglacial aeolian sands of the Whyalla Sandstone on the Stuart Shelf. Next, melting of the icecaps and climatic warming led to deposition of a cap dolomite, the Nuccaleena Formation, which intertongues with the tidal flat Seacliff Sandstone that marks the base of the Wilpena Group. Rapid marine transgression followed and a coarsening-upwards succession of shelf, deltaic and tidal flat sediments (Brachina Formation and ABC Range Quartzite in the Adelaide Geosyncline; Tent Hill Formation on the Stuart Shelf) was deposited. A second transgression, only recorded in the Adelaide Geosyncline, led to the deposition of the Bunyeroo Formation in a subtidal-mudflat environment, followed by a prograding calcareous clastic sequence, the Wonoka Formation, deposited on the continental shelf. During deposition of the Wonoka Formation major canyons were incised into the lower Wonoka Formation, Bunyeroo Formation and ABC Range Quartzite at Pichi Richi and Waukarie Creek, and these extend onto Cultana. The Neoproterozoic sediments in the Adelaide Geosyncline were deformed by the Cambrian- Ordovician Delamerian Orogeny (~ 515–480 Ma). Deformation took the form of N-S trending, N plunging upright folds, with an axial-planar cleavage developed in silt and shale lithologies such as the Brachina and Angepena Formations. The folds are dissected by N-S trending reverse and strike-slip faults which predominantly dip steeply to the west. Faults are defined by a more strongly developed cleavage in siltstone and shale lithologies and a blocky cleavage or jointing in arenaceous lithologies, as well as quartz veining with slickensides and tension gashes. Deformation did not extend to the Stuart Shelf, and the Torrens Hinge served as a transitional zone of deformation between it and the deformed Adelaide Geosyncline, accommodating strain via thrusting and gentle folding. Thrusting along the Cultana Fault may have occurred at this time. In the early Jurassic, kimberlitic magma intruded the Tent Hill Formation south of El Alamein, an event associated with the rifting of Australia and Gondwana. Following the complete separation of Australia from Antarctica, marine transgression over the southern part of South Australia led to the formation of the Late Eocene to Pleistocene Pirie Basin, containing shallow marine, lagoonal and lacustrine sediments. During the Pleistocene, clays, sands and gravels of the Hindmarsh Clay were deposited in alluvial fan, valley flat and playa lake environments flanking the Flinders Ranges and extending westwards beneath the Baroota Plain and Spencer Gulf. The alluvial fan building was followed by four marine transgressions beyond the Spencer Gulf (creating the ‘older Pleistocene marine beds’, Mambray Formation, False Bay Formation and Lowly Point Formation), each separated by marine regression and a period of sub-aerial exposure and pedogenesis. The younger alluvial fans now flanking the western margin of the Flinders Ranges were subsequently deposited, as well as the alluvial fans and extensive distal sheetwash fans and plains surrounding the Simmens Plateau. These alluvial deposits are partly contemporaneous with the extensive aeolian sands which built up on the coastal plain around the Spencer Gulf. During the Holocene, the peritidal sediments of the Saint Kilda Formation were deposited in the Spencer Gulf. In terrestrial environments during the Holocene, fluvial sedimentation and erosion continues in modern channels draining the Flinders Ranges and Simmens Plateau, and saline playa deposits are forming at the head of False Bay. High-angle slope deposits have formed and continue to form along the steep flanks of the prominent ridges along the western edge of the southern Flinders Ranges. Cultana has potential to host economic mineral deposits arising from the actions of a number of mineralising styles, particularly those associated with emplacement of the Hiltaba Suite – Gawler Range Volcanics (~1590–1575 Ma), such as IOCG-U, Pb-Zn skarn or epithermal mineralisation. Potential exists too for base metal mineralisation within the Neoproterozoic sediments on the Stuart Shelf and in the Adelaide Geosyncline, as the Myall Creek copper prospect contains Cu-Pb-Zn-Ag mineralisation at the unconformity between the Tapley Hill Formation and Pandurra Formation. The Pandurra Formation (~1575 Ma) in the Cariewerloo Basin is also thought to potentially host unconformity-related uranium. In addition, a number of extractive resources have been sourced from Cultana, including evaporites, dimension stone and aggregate, clay, sand and gravel.

title: Cultana, South Australia. Sheet 6432, International Index. 1:100 000 Geological Series digital map.
notes:
Notes: This map is a product of work undertaken by the Geological Survey of South Australia (GSSA)as part of a current mapping programme aiming to revise and publish a second edition of the PORT AUGUSTA 1:250 000 mapsheet.
Geographic Locality: North-eastern Eyre Peninsula;Cultana Hills;Cultana Army Land;Lincoln Highway;Northern Spencer Gulf;Whyalla;False Bay;Port Augusta;South-western Flinders Ranges;Stirling North;Nectar Brook;Mambray Creek

abstract: Cultana is located on parts of the north-eastern Eyre Peninsula, northern Spencer Gulf and south-western Flinders Ranges, and is underlain by rocks of the Mesoarchaean-Mesoproterozoic Gawler Craton, the Neoproterozoic Adelaide Geosyncline, Torrens Hinge Zone and Stuart Shelf, and the Tertiary Pirie Basin.  In a tectonostratigraphic sense, Cultana lies at the junction of a number of geological provinces. The area to the west of the Spencer Gulf is part of the Gawler Craton; a Mesoarchaean to early Mesoproterozoic geological province consisting of metamorphosed sediments and volcanic and intrusive igneous rocks deformed during the Sleafordian Orogeny (~2440 Ma), Cornian Orogeny (~1850 Ma), Kimban Orogeny (~1730–1690 Ma), and Kararan Orogeny (~1590–1555 Ma). The eastern margin of the Gawler Craton is overlain by the Cariewerloo Basin, a middle to late Mesoproterozoic intracratonic basin which accommodated the red beds of the Pandurra Formation. The rocks exposed in the Flinders Ranges are part of the Adelaide Geosyncline, a sequence of Neoproterozoic to early Cambrian sediments and basic volcanic rocks deposited in a rift basin, which were subsequently folded and faulted during the Cambro-Ordovician Delamerian Orogeny. The Stuart Shelf overlies the Cariewerloo Basin and Gawler Craton and consists of a sequence of undeformed Neoproterozoic sediments correlative with parts of the Adelaide Geosyncline. The Torrens Hinge Zone, a transitional zone of gentle folding and faulting, separates the strongly deformed sediments of the Adelaide Geosyncline from their undeformed counterparts on the Stuart Shelf. The Tertiary Pirie Basin lies beneath the northern Spencer Gulf, and contains marine sediments.

This report represents the annual and final surrender report for Exploration Licence 6929 "South Gap" for the period 07/09/2023 to 07/11/2024. The tenement is comprised of 3 blocks and is located approximately 85 km north west of Port Augusta on the Stuart Shelf, in the eastern Gawler Craton. The area is primarily considered prospective for possible sediment hosted copper, while a secondary target is iron oxide copper gold style mineralisation within the Proterozoic basement. 

The company did not undertake any field activities during the reporting period, with time spent reviewing open file data from previous exploration reports. Bouguer Gravity and TMI images were prepared by Allender Exploration Services and were reviewed to assist in the interpretation of the structural and basement geology. No targets for sediment hosted copper were identified, nor did the review of previous exploration data provide sufficient encouragement to continue exploration on the tenement, as such the decision was made to relinquish the area.

name: d20011614
title: RB 2016/00014 Geology of the Six Mile Hill 1:75 000 Special Edition Map Sheet.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Southern Gawler Ranges;Roopena Station;Six Mile Hill;Uno Fault;Roopena Fault;Randell Fault;Wizzo Well Fault;Trevor Fault;Angle Dam Fault;Red Rock Fault
Doc No: RB 2016/00014
Drillhole: DDH MSDP01 - DDH MSDP04;(287995 - 287998)
abstract: The Six Mile Hill 1:75 000 Map Sheet was produced as part of a mapping program integrated into the Mineral Systems Drilling Program (MSDP) along the southern margin of the Gawler Ranges. The objective of the mapping program was to provide a regional geological context in which the stratigraphy, alteration and mineralisation of rocks revealed by the MSDP drilling could be interpreted, and comprised detailed basement, structural and regolith mapping. This report comprises the Explanatory Notes to the Six Mile Hill Map Sheet, part of the Mineral Systems Drilling Program Special Map Series.  Six Mile Hill spans a number of geological provinces, including the Mesoarchaean-Mesoproterozoic Gawler Craton, the Mesoproterozoic Cariewerloo Basin and the Neoproterozoic Stuart Shelf, as well as preserving a protracted history of deposition in the Cenozoic. The earliest history of the area is recorded by a phase of basin development in the late Palaeoproterozoic, comprising the deposition of the Broadview Schist, and emplacement of the Wire Dam Dolerite and Tip Top Granite, accompanied by solid-state deformation between c. 1790 and 1775 Ma. Further sedimentation occurred at c. 1755 Ma, comprising deposition of the Moonabie and Wandearah formations. This was followed by intrusion of the Moola Suite at c. 1745 Ma, and basin inversion during the Kimban Orogeny (c. 1740–1690 Ma), which comprised low temperature fabric development and the formation of mylonites and thrust faults during west-southwest-directed shortening. Open folding of the Moonabie Formation during northeast-directed shortening may have occurred during the Kimban Orogeny or early during the Kararan Orogeny (c. 1610–1590 Ma). This was followed by eruption of extrusive and pyroclastic felsic volcanics and subaerial and subaqueous basaltic lavas of the Gawler Range Volcanics during the early Mesoproterozoic (c. 1590 Ma). The Gawler Craton was overlain by fluvial red beds of the Pandurra Formation at c. 1420 Ma, and was subsequently subject to weathering and erosion until the Neoproterozoic. Deposition of sediments on the Stuart Shelf commenced at c. 825 Ma with fluvial sediments of the Backy Point Formation interlayered with subaerial basaltic lavas of the Beda Basalt, and intrusion of the Gairdner Dolerite in the Gawler Craton. The Stuart Shelf was subject to exposure and erosion until c. 645 Ma when there was marine transgression and deposition of the Tapley Hill Formation. This was followed by localised deposition of fluvio-deltaic to shallow marine facies of the Upalinna and Yerelina subgroups, including the Whyalla Sandstone, and then post-glacial transgression and deposition of the Tent Hill Formation after c. 635 Ma. Six Mile Hill was subject to weathering and erosion during the Palaeozoic and Mesozoic, after which it records deep weathering, silicification and ferruginisation, as well as the deposition of colluvial, alluvial and aeolian deposits during the Cenozoic, and neotectonic faulting.

name: rb8800051
title: RB 88/00051 Pre-Mesozoic geology of the Curdimurka region.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Willouran Ranges
Doc No: RB 88/00051
abstract: Pre-Mesozoic rocks are best exposed in the Willouran Ranges SW of Marree, but inliers occur as far west as Stuart Creek. These approximate the junction of the Stuart Shelf (to the west) with the Torrens Hinge Zone, which extends east to the Norwest Fault, the western edge of the Adelaide Geosyncline. Oldest rocks of the geosyncline are the Callanna Group, over 6000 metres of partly evaporitic rocks with a lower basaltic flow, and a thin dacite with U-Pb zircon age of 802 + / - 10 Ma. Overlying sequences are the Burra Group, over 9000 metres of partly intertidal clastics and carbonates; Umberatana Group, over 3000 metres of glacial and marine sediments, and Wilpena Group of over 1500 metres of predominantly intertidal clastics. The ranges are cut by NW-trending fracture zones, paralleling Delamerian (early Palaeozoic) folds, accompanied by intrusive, partly diapiric, breccias. Minor copper deposits are mainly related to quartz-carbonate veins just outside breccia zones.

name: rb8900041
title: RB 89/00041 Re-assessment of 1000-1200 Ma ages from the Musgrave Block to the Willyama Inliers.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Wearing Hills;Lake Torrens;Tommie Wattie Bore
Doc No: RB 89/00041
Drillhole: Mallabie 1;Reedy Lagoon 1;Phillips Ridge PD2;Crocker Well EC12;Crocker Well EC50;Delhi-Aquitaine BDH2
abstract: Ages between 1000 and 1200 Ma have been recorded from diverse rock types at 10 scattered localities outside the Musgrave Block and Ammaroodinna Inlier. All are K-Ar and Rb-Sr mineral concentrates or whole rock ages, except 1 U-Pb age on detrital zircons from the Bunyeroo Formation, Wearing Hills. Samples outside the Musgrave Block which exhibit solely thermal updating are found in the Peake and Denison Inliers, Mount Painter Inliers, Willyama Inliers and the Stuart Shelf. This thermal event is apparently synchronous with emplacement of the Gairdner Dyke Swarm and extrusion of the Beda Volcanics. All 3 are apparently synchronous and manifestations of a major phase of crustal extension - best dated at 1070 +/- 74 Ma. This report collates and interprets data in terms of more widespread effects of the Musgravian Orogeny and thermal resetting during a subsequent period of crustal extension.

name: rb9500041
title: RB 95/00041 Commodity review. Copper and gold in South Australia.
notes:
Geographic Locality: South Australia
Doc No: RB 95/00041
abstract: The giant Olympic Dam deposit has a total resource of about 2 200 million tonnes grading 1.4% Cu, 0.5 kg/t U3O8, 0.5 g/t Au and 3.1 g/t Ag.  Development of Olympic Dam, with current annual production of 67 000 t of copper and further expansion planned, again makes South Australia a major copper producer as in the late nineteenth century.  Other important producing mines have included Kapunda, Burra, Wallaroo, Moonta, Kanmantoo and Mt Gunson.  Olympic Dam is associated with Proterozoic Hiltaba Suite granite and Gawler Range Volcanics.  These units are widespread on the Gawler Craton and potential for further discoveries is high.  Proterozoic rocks of the Gawler Craton and Curnamona Province are also prospective for Cu-Au type mineralisation as found in the eastern Mt Isa Block, Qld, and in Tennant Creek, NT.  Adelaidean and Cambrian rocks of the Adelaide Geosyncline and Stuart Shelf host numerous, widespread copper occurrences and there is good potential for discovery of further stratiform or structurally controlled deposits.  There is also potential for development of low cost, heap leaching operations.  The state has many gold workings, particularly in the Adelaide Geosyncline and Tarcoola regions, but total production has been small.  However, Olympic Dam is a major gold resource and the potential for discovery of further Proterozoic gold-copper and gold-only deposits is considerable.  Archaean terranes of the northwest Gawler Craton have recently been shown to include mafic-ultramafic suites enhancing similarities to gold bearing Archaean greenstone belts elsewhere.  Across much of South Australia extensive soil and sediment cover blanketing basement rocks has hampered exploration.  Airborne geophysics and drilling undertaken as part of the South Australian Exploration Initiative and Broken Hill Exploration Initiative have highlighted the prospectivity of many areas and will be a key factor in future exploration.

Recent mine production includes willemite (zinc silicate) from Puttupa and silver as a by-product from operations at Cattlegrid and Olympic Dam. Port Pirie was established as the seaport for the massive lead-zinc-silver deposit discovered at Broken Hill in 1883. The combined lead-zinc-silver smelting and refining facility at Port Pirie is the world's largest lead refiner but depends primarily on concentrates from Broken Hill which has an estimated mine life of 20 years. Significant indigenous resources must be identified to ensure the long term viability of Port Pirie.

name: rb5900138
title: RB 59/00138 Lower boundary of the Adelaide system and older basement relationships in SA.
notes:
Notes: 64/00433A
Geographic Locality: South Australia
Doc No: RB 59/00138 p: na
abstract: The stratigraphic problem of defining the lower boundary of the Adelaide System is discussed in relation to the geology of several critical areas in the Adelaide Geosyncline and adjacent shelf platform. The Precambrian stratigraphic succession and geological history is outlined with the aid of Rb/Sr age determinations made by W. Compston of Australian National University. It is concluded that the lower boundary of the Adelaide System is related to the collapse of older basement positive areas on which had developed a regional erosional surface. The surface is defined by the Callanna Beds, the oldest deposits of Willouran age. Willouran sedimentation began sometime between 1340m and 1490m years. Erosion of the basement rocks probably occupied a major earlier part of this time interval.

abstract: Critical minerals are a collection of metal and non-metal commodities considered essential for economic and industrial development, and for which there are significant concerns around future supply due to resource scarcity or geopolitical factors. The Geological Survey of South Australia's Critical Minerals South Australia (CMSA) project focuses on advancing knowledge to support critical minerals discovery and exploration in South Australia. The Report Book includes: - Overview of uses for manganese - Review of economic manganese deposit types - Manganese occurrences and prospectivity in South Australia - Maps of South Australia’s manganese occurrences and characteristic magnesium forms - Excel spreadsheet combining all occurrence data for manganese available from South Australia’s Mineral Deposit (MinDep) database.

abstract: The eastern Gawler Craton hosts the giant Olympic Dam iron oxide - associated copper-gold (IOCG) deposit, as well as several other world class IOCG deposits (i.e. Prominent Hill and Carrapateena). The region is covered by a thick sequence of Mesoproterozoic to Cenozoic sedimentary and volcanic rocks, making the region difficult and costly to explore using conventional methods. Sets of high quality geoscientific data from the eastern Gawler Craton, such as magnetic, gravity, seismic, radiometric, geological, geochemical, geochronological and hyperspectral data, have been systematically acquired by the Geological Survey of South Australia. Previously these datasets had been looked at independently of each other. Now, however, modern 3D geological mapping and data integration techniques have been adopted by the authors to produce a common earth model of the Emmie Bluff IOCG prospect, that can be readily updated as new data become available. By using this common earth model in conjunction with an understanding of IOCG mineral systems, future explorationists will be able predict where the particular data they are observing lies both spatially and conceptually within the alteration/mineralising system. There are two different styles of IOCG mineral systems which have been active in the eastern Gawler Craton: haematite-dominated systems on the Stuart Shelf, and magnetite-dominated systems on the Yorke Peninsula. For the subject model, UBC gravity and magnetic inversions have been used to map haematite and magnetite alteration in three dimensions, using the method outlined by Williams and Chopping (2009). Chemical modelling of these IOCG mineral systems suggests that high grade mineralisation is likely to form at the haematite/magnetite transition, but the bulk of the mineralisation should occur largely within the haematite zone (Bastrokov, et al., 2007). Multi-element geochemical and spectral mineralogy data have been used to characterise the distribution and degree of development of sericite, chlorite, albite and K-feldspar alteration

For the subject model, UBC gravity and magnetic inversions have been used to map haematite and magnetite alteration in three dimensions, using the method outlined by Williams and Chopping (2009). Chemical modelling of these IOCG mineral systems suggests that high grade mineralisation is likely to form at the haematite/magnetite transition, but the bulk of the mineralisation should occur largely within the haematite zone (Bastrokov, et al., 2007). Multi-element geochemical and spectral mineralogy data have been used to characterise the distribution and degree of development of sericite, chlorite, albite and K-feldspar alteration.

title: RB 81/00001 Progress report on the geology of the Curdimurka region.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Curdimurka
Doc No: RB 81/00001
abstract: Geology is summarised based on literature and recent geological mapping. The Adelaidean outcrops in the Willouran Ranges where it is folded, fractured and cut by partly diapiric crush zones. The oldest Adelaidean, Callanna Beds, occurs as blocks in diapirs and as an evaporitic sequence over 5000 metres thick. The Burra Group is over 7000 metres thick, overlain unconformably by the partly glacial Umberatana Group (7000 metres) and the Wilpena Group (over 400 metres). Much of the area is covered by Cretaceous shales and sands, and Cainozoic fluvial to lacustrine carbonates, sands and evaporites, and near Lake Eyre, the Etadunna Formation. The most important mineral resource is artesian water. Minor epigenetic copper is common in the Precambrian associated with crush zones.

name: rb6300135
title: RB 63/00135 Geology of the Cultana 1:63 360 map area (revised version of RB 56/17).
notes:
Notes: Published in South Australia. geological survey. report of investigations sadme, vol. 34, 34 pages; maps, illust 62/01935
Geographic Locality: Spencer Gulf;Cultana;Whyalla
Doc No: RB 63/00135
abstract: The Cultana map area lies about 150 miles north-northeast of Adelaide and straddles the narrow northern arm of Spencer Golf, South Australia. Along the western side of the area, which includes the industrial town of Whyalla, are exposures of steeply folded dark sandstone of the Moonabie Formation (pre- Adelaide System lower Precambrian) overlain by the Pandurra Formation, reddish sandstone of possible Willouran (lower Adelaide System) age. These rocks are exposed again along the western shore of Spencer Gulf, where the Moonabie Formation is intruded by the Cultana Granite. Lavas considered to be equivalent to the Roopena Level (about 1 450 million years old) are here interbedded with the Pandurra Formation.  Flat-lying quartzite of the Tent Hill Formation, which forms a prominent mesa west of Spencer Gulf, is probably of Marinoan (upper Adelaidean System) age and overlies the poorly-outcropping Tregolana Shale. These little-disturbed beds of the Stuart Stable Shelf contrast with their equivalent geosynclinals facies which appears as steeply-dipping quartzites and shales of the Wilpena and Umberatana Groups of the Adelaide System in the western edge of the Flinders Ranges, northeast corner of the map area. Much of the map area is covered by outwash, sand and swamp deposits.

abstract: It is proposed to construct a new road bridge across Spencer Gulf at Port Augusta, on an alignment south of the existing Great Western Road Bridge.  Geological investigations, mainly cable-tool have shown up to 95 ft of sediments of Tertiary to Recent age, in a downfaulted trough, overlying bedrock of Proterozoic (Marinoan) Age. There are no geological problems likely to affect the feasibility of the project. There is no advantage geologically in any other alignment than the one adopted. title: RB 2023/00038 Quantitative Mineral Resource Assessment of undiscovered sedimentary-hosted copper in South Australia.
abstract: Sedimentary-hosted copper deposits are the second most important source of copper in the world with most South Australian sediment-hosted copper occurrences located within the Adelaide Rift Complex, Torrens Hinge Zone and Stuart Shelf. In response to the growing need for more copper, the Geological Survey of South Australia conducted a Quantitative mineral-resource assessment (QMRA) based on a well-defined global grade-tonnage model. The QMRA is a project to develop and test methods of assessing potential for undiscovered mineral resources within South Australia. The QMRA helps to outline the principal areas in South Australia that have potential for undiscovered sedimentary-hosted copper and to estimate the probable amounts of sedimentary-hosted copper to a depth of 1 kilometre below the surface. Helping to provide a framework for reducing uncertainty and supporting decisions concerning potential mineral resources.

abstract: The sedimentary environment of Cambrian and Marinoan shelf sediments in South Australia is outlined. Tables are presented showing the distribution of Cu and Pb in the various facies of these sediments. Low grade copper mineralisation in some Marinoan shale and dolomite units is considered to be contemporaneous with sedimentation. The extensive enrichment of Pb in basal Cambrian sediments is attributed to either a sedimentary exhalative process contemporaneous with sedimentation, or later telethermal mineralisation related to an Ordovician orogeny. Basement fault-shear lineaments and areas of Pb and Cu enrichment are inter-related.

name: mesac27800
title: AusLAMP magnetotelluric survey - data subset [plus processing results for the PACE Copper - funded, Gawler Craton survey portion]. Data package.
notes:
Notes: Data package Version 1.  Usage limitations: caution should be taken when interpreting structures at depths less than ~10 km or greater than ~200 km, as model sensitivities are low in these depth ranges. MT survey station positional accuracy is given to ~100 m.
Geographic Locality: West-central, south-central and east-central South Australia
Doc No: GDP 00090
abstract: The Australian Lithospheric Architecture Magnetotelluric Project (AusLAMP) is a major new geophysical research program that is under way to map the electrical resistivity structure of the continental lithosphere, by utilising deep-sounding magnetotelluric (MT) data that is being progressively acquired via an eventual continent-wide deployment of long-period (10-10 000 s) magnetotelluric instruments in a half-degree interval (~55 km) grid of stations set across all of Australia. AusLAMP aims to provide constraints on the tectonic evolution of the continent and its hidden mineral exploration potential, as part of the UNCOVER initiative.   Areas covered by this subset of the survey include the Mesoproterozoic Coompana Province, the mineral-rich Archaean-Proterozoic Gawler Craton that is in part buried beneath cover of the Neoproterozoic Stuart Shelf that extends across to the east to cover the Neoproterozoic Ikara-Flinders Ranges, and the western portion of the Palaeo-Mesoproterozoic Curnamona Province.  The central Gawler Craton is imaged as a resistive zone having conductive margins which  surround the core of the cratonic block at shallow upper mantle depths.  The results of the inversions of the AusLAMP data highlight the correlative significance of using them in combination with geochemical data to generate fertility vectors for mineral systems.

abstract: Small quantities of precious opal have been mined from sediments of the Early Cretaceous Marree Formation at Stuart Creek, 50 km north of Andamooka. name: rb7900114
title: RB 79/00114 Palaeodrainage systems in western South Australia. Their detection by Landsat imagery, stratigraphic significance and economic potential.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Great Victoria Desert;Nullarbor
Doc No: RB 79/00114
abstract: Two major palaeodrainage systems of Tertiary age, with watersheds of up to 35 000 square km and channel lengths of 200-250 km, have been recognised and delineated using LANDSAT imagery, during 1:250 000 scale geological mapping in western South Australia. These systems have been termed the Tallaringa Palaeodrainage System and Mirackina Palaeochannel. The former is largely intact and still forms a subtle valley, appearing as a pale-toned, branching feature on satellite imagery. The channel-fill of the latter has been silicified and ferruginised, and through erosion has been exhumed, to form, today, a duricrust capping to an isolated, sinuous line of mesas. It is prominent as a dark feature on the imagery due to the ferruginisation. LANDSAT imagery, reconnaissance-geological and barometric altitude data has been subsequently used to develop a preliminary interpretation of Tertiary palaeodrainage throughout western South Australia, and of Tertiary palaeogeography on the north-eastern margin of the Eucla Basin. The systems are of economic interest: they are potentially useful aquifers and hosts to heavy mineral placer deposits; contain large volumes of low-grade lignite and medium-grade palygorskite-type clays; and contain sediments which are lithologically similar and stratigraphically equivalent to channel-confined hosts to economic uranium mineralisation both at Lake Frome and Yeelirrie.  While the two palaeodrainage systems described in detail have been eroded and/or leached to a greater or lesser degree, they serve to indicate the possible sediment content and consequent mineral potential of other systems in the region. The definition of palaeodrainage patterns will therefore be prerequisite to assessing the overall mineral potential of the province and to primary geological mapping of the region. The use of LANDSAT imagery and complementary techniques for this purpose has been demonstrated, and it is clear that it will be an important tool for ensuring the success of such programmes in the future.

abstract: Refraction and experimental reflection seismic shooting was undertaken in EL 190 on Roxby Downs Station during May 1975, along 3 lines totalling 13.2 line km.  The aim was to map Cambrian and Precambrian sedimentary horizons using methods generally applied in areas of younger sediments. A refraction horizon probably correlatable with unweathered Cambrian Andamooka Limestone was mapped along two lines, mostly at a depth of less than 40 metres below the surface. Interpretation of the single fold reflection data is very difficult, but one tentative horizon in the vicinity of Olympic Dam at a depth of about 300 metres below surface has been mapped over a distance of 1 km. abstract: This inaugural regolith map of the southern Gawler Ranges margin provides a valuable regional overview of the main regolith types and their associated landforms, plus a general outline of the major areas of bedrock or regolith-dominated terrain, as well as spatial information about the occurrence of in-situ versus transported regolith. A major challenge that bedrock mineral explorers face in many parts of South Australia is how to explore efficiently and effectively through extensive and thick regolith cover. abstract: Critical minerals are a collection of metal and non-metal commodities considered essential for economic and industrial development, and for which there are significant concerns around future supply due to resource scarcity or geopolitical factors. The Geological Survey of South Australia's Critical Minerals South Australia (CMSA) project focuses on advancing knowledge to support critical minerals discovery and exploration in South Australia.  The CMSA project, through the "Critical mineral potential of South Australia" report book series, reviews and identifies key mineralisation styles for defined critical minerals, maps existing critical mineral occurrences across the State and identifies regions with significant critical mineral potential aiming to increase industry and investor understanding of South Australia's critical mineral potential.  The Report Book includes: - Overview of uses for magnesium - Review of economic magnesium deposit types - Magnesium occurrences and prospectivity in South Australia - Maps of South Australia’s magnesium occurrences and characteristic magnesium forms - Excel spreadsheet combining all occurrence data for magnesium available from South Australia’s Mineral Deposit (MinDep) database.

abstract: Thirty core trays containing confidential diamond drillcore that is representative of company exploration drillhole RD 16 located at Olympic Dam [hole total depth 1318.9 m] were provided by EL 536 licensee Western Mining Corp. Ltd and placed on public display from May to October, 1979, by the South Australian Department of Mines and Energy.  The opportunity to inspect the core and to obtain an early stage insight to the lithologies and mineralisation at the recently discovered giant Olympic Dam Cu-U-Au deposit was greatly appreciated by all geoscientists.  The mechanics of establishing this unprecedented display and of conducting core inspection visits are described, the technical observations of about 350 visitors are summarised, and various conclusions have been drawn concerning some successes and shortcomings of the exercise, for application to possible future displays.  Significant outcomes from making the display and facilitating visitor interpretations are the apparent general lack of feature correlation with any other known deposit (with the possible exception of Mount Painter) and the lack of consensus on the mode of origin for both the mineralisation and host rocks.  Most models involve elements of contemporaneous sedimentation, volcanism, high-level plutonism and hydrothermal activity.

abstract:
The Copper Coast Project is located along the eastern flank of the Spencer Gulf, extending from Port Augusta in the north to Port Wakefield in the south and Gladstone in the east. The Copper Coast Project is located along the eastern margin of the Gawler Craton in South Australia and covers Proterozoic rocks of the Stuart Shelf, Torrens Hinge Zone, and Adelaide Rift Complex, which form part of the Adelaide Superbasin. The project currently comprises of 5 tenements (EL 6551 & EL 6561 to EL 6564), covering approximately 3,455 km2.

Exploration completed on the Copper Coast Project during the reporting period comprised a hydrogeochemical sampling program and an airborne electromagnetic survey. A further 13 hydrogeochemical samples were collected across Els 6561, 6562 and 6564 as part of a resampling and infill survey. The company believe that the work completed in the reporting period reinforced the presence of the earlier identified geochemical anomalies in the hydrogeochemical surveys, though at lower concentrations thought to be related to dilution due to increased rainfall preceding sampling.

The TEMPEST airborne EM survey was flown June-July 2024 at 1000 m line spacing, with 568 line-km flown over EL 6551, 400.8 line-km flown over EL 6561, and 17.3 line-km flown over EL 6562.   While the airborne EM survey effectively mapped the carbonate stratigraphy and cover, it did not reveal conductive anomalies, indicating limited potential for massive sulfide mineralisation in the surveyed areas.

title: RB 2016/00013 Geological field excursion guide — Rifts, reverse faults and regolith: Neoproterozoic to Cenozoic geology in the Mid-North of South Australia.
notes:
Notes: A guidebook that was originally provided to AESC participants who had enrolled to go on a post-conference field trip to the Mid-North of South Australia, which took place on 1-2 July 2016.
Geographic Locality: Northern Mount Lofty Ranges;Mallala;Owen;Redbanks;Spring Gully;Rochester;Yacka;Bundaleer;River Broughton;Spalding;Clare;Farrell Flat;Burra;Worlds End;Burra Creek
Doc No: RB 2016/00013
abstract: The rolling hills, wheat paddocks and vineyards of the Mid-North region of South Australia conceal a geological transition between the Adelaide Hills and the Flinders Ranges. Here the landscape is subtly controlled by the Neoproterozoic bedrock geology, Delamerian deformational structures, neotectonics, and regolith development. The bedrock of the Mount Lofty Ranges, Mid-North and Flinders Ranges consists of Neoproterozoic and Cambrian sedimentary and minor igneous rocks deposited in a complex of rift and sag basins, traditionally known as the Adelaide Geosyncline (Sprigg, 1952; Preiss, 1987). Thin platformal equivalents overlying the eastern Gawler Craton comprise the Stuart Shelf, while the Torrens Hinge Zone is an openly folded zone of transition between the Stuart Shelf and Adelaide Geosyncline. In the Mid-North, rifting occurring at ~800 Ma produced regional north-south trending graben structures that became filled with very thick siliciclastic and carbonate successions of the Callanna Group and Burra Group, this deposition being interspersed by minor mafic and rare felsic magmatism. The Burra Group is unconformably overlain by the Umberatana Group, this sequence commencing with widespread glaciomarine and fluvioglacial deposits of Sturtian age. Subsequent Neoproterozoic sedimentation of the upper Umberatana and Wilpena Groups was less rift-controlled, and includes deposits of the Elatina glaciation of Marinoan age. Delamerian folding and thrusting in the mid-Cambrian involved northwest- to west-directed transport and sinistral transpression, and set up the tectonic framework for neotectonic reactivation when the Australian continent became subject to east-west compression in the Cenozoic. Ancient weathering surfaces and regolith profiles were uplifted and dissected, and terrestrial to marine Tertiary basins formed on both sides of the highlands, with Quaternary alluvial deposits flanking the ranges.  The excursion will visit representative sections of the Callanna Group and Burra Group, Sturtian and Marinoan glacial deposits, evidence of Delamerian thrusting and folding, neotectonic reverse faulting, Cenozoic marine and terrestrial sediments and regolith profiles, and two of South Australia’s historic copper mines at Burra and Kapunda.  Much of the visited region (the BURRA 1:250,000 map sheet area, bounded by latitudes 33°S and 34°S, and longitudes 138°00’ E and 138°30’ E) was mapped in detail by the excursion leaders during the period 1988-2001, and compiled map data (100K geology) is downloadable through SARIG.

title: RB 2016/00024 Mineral Systems Drilling Program Rock Shack - [a pictorial catalogue of the] outcrop sample collection for the MSDP southern Gawler Ranges margin.
notes:

abstract: Between July 2015 and April 2016, the Geological Survey of South Australia, in collaboration with the Deep Exploration Technologies Cooperative Research Centre (DET CRC), Minotaur Exploration Limited and Kingston Resources Limited, carried out a Mineral Systems Drilling Program (MSDP) diamond drilling campaign along the southern margin of the Gawler Ranges. Working in concert with this drilling campaign, a detailed geological mapping program was carried out at each of the three drilling target areas, namely, Six Mile Hill, Peltabinna and Mount Double, in order to provide a regional geological context into which the stratigraphy and potentially the alteration and mineralisation of the drillholes can be interpreted. This geological mapping program comprised detailed basement, structural and regolith mapping, as well as petrological, whole rock geochemical, isotopic and geochronological studies, with a particular focus on the stratigraphy of the lower Gawler Range Volcanics. During the mapping program, samples of outcropping rocks were collected for future studies of their petrology, geochemistry and geochronology, which samples also included hand specimens intended for comparison with the lithologies encountered in drill cores recovered from the MSDP drillholes.  This report comprises a photographic catalogue of nearly 100 selected rock sample hand specimens collected during the geological mapping program. These were displayed during the MSDP Open Day held on 11 August 2016, and are intended to be displayed during Discovery Day on 1 December 2016, both of which events are hosted by the Geological Survey of South Australia (GSSA) and the Department of State Development (DSD). The majority of the rock samples have been cross-referenced to detailed geological mapping which the authors of this report conducted in each of the three MSDP drilling areas located along the southern margin of the Gawler Range Volcanic Province: these newly mapped areas lie within the Six Mile Hill, Peltabinna and Mount Double 1:75,000 scale special geological map sheet extents. A few of the rock samples were obtained from adjacent map sheet areas.

abstract: During the period 4 March to 22 June 2017, most of the TORRENS 1:250k map sheet area was flown under contract to the SA Government and Geoscience Australia as part of the PACE Copper Gawler Craton Airborne Survey. The intent of this survey overall [it is still in progress] is to capture approximately 1.8 million flight line km of new geophysical data (magnetic, radiometric and digital elevation model data) over an area of approximately 324,000 square km.  The Region 3B survey coverage as completed has amounted to 82,808 line km, acquired using a fixed wing aircraft instrument platform. Flight paths consisted of principal east-west orientated survey lines spaced 200 m apart, tied by orthogonal lines spaced 2 km apart, and the geophysical data was read using a 60 m mean sensor height above the ground surface.  In terms of product deliverables provided by the survey contractor, the aeromagnetic data include TMI, TMI reduced-to-pole, and 1VD of RTP TMI; the elevation data include models derived from radar altimeter and laser altimeter, subtracted from differential GPS heights; and the spectrometer data include dose rate, uranium, thorium, potassium and ternary (RGB) radiometric datasets. These digital data have been stored by the clients as either located XYZ data (ascii) or Grid Exchange Format (GXF) data presented via ERMapper grids or tif images.

abstract: HyLogging systems, and the PIMA and ASD field spectrometers (Terraspec, Labspec and Fieldspec), are a generation of analysis instruments which provide rapid and cost effective data on sample mineralogy and on mineral characteristics.  Spectral analysis has applications in:  - Delineating alteration systems;  - Understanding alteration - mineralisation relationships;  - Target generation;  - Tackling grade control problems;  - Identifying overburden/bedrock boundaries. IR technology is ideally suited to alteration mapping, and over recent years spectral analysis has been effectively applied worldwide to mineral exploration and the characterisation of rock alteration mineralogy suites.  The important characteristics of field spectrometers include:  - Laboratory quality spectral data of minerals, permitting the determination of fine spectral details, such as crystallinity variations and elemental substitution.  - An internal light source in most cases, no restrictions on location or time of day;  - Each measurement requires no sample preparation (although samples need to be dry);  - Spectra are acquired in ~3-60 seconds, allowing the rapid collection of a large number of analyses in a short time frame;  - Instant display of spectra on PC/palmtop screen;  - Measurements can be made of all types of samples, including diamond drill core, RC and RAB chips, and outcrop and soil samples, and selective measurements may be made of in situ veins, breccia fragments and small-scale alteration zoning (provided that samples are dry).

title: RB 2007/00021 Compilation of SHRIMP U-Pb geochronological data for the Gawler Craton, South Australia, 2007.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Investigator Group of islands;Pearson Islands;Flinders Island;Seal Point;Mount Woods district;Spire Hill;Moonlight Hill
Doc No: RB 2007/00021
abstract: This Report Book contains zircon U-Pb geochronological data obtained between December 2006 and June 2007, for rock samples derived from the Gawler Craton of South Australia. The geochronological study was undertaken as part of the National Geoscience Agreement, as a collaborative research programme conducted between the Commonwealth's Division of Minerals and Energy, the Department of Primary Industries and Resources, South Australia, and Geoscience Australia. The aim of the programme is to provide geochronological constraints on geodynamic and tectonic models for geological provinces of South Australia, and to help develop an improved geological and metallogenic geoscientific framework for these provinces. The subject document is a technical report describing samples analysed and the analytical results obtained for the Gawler Craton in Year 2 of the research collaboration, with a brief discussion of their geochronological interpretation. The broader geological implications of the data will later be published elsewhere. The complete data files, including data for the QGNG and Temora analytical standards, will be stored in the Geoscience Australia database, OZCHRON. A tabulated summary of the U-Pb zircon ages obtained in this study is presented herein, with supporting information about the sample processing, separated zircon grain morphology, geochronological data reduction, data presentation and contamination checking. Also included is background information about the field geological relationships of the rock samples studied, explaining the rationale for selection of the samples, plus their petrological descriptions and petrogenetic interpretations.

abstract: This regolith material hand specimen atlas displays 246 images of 212 regolith samples which have been collected over the last 30 years by the authors, present and past Geological Survey of South Australia (GSSA) staff and members of the Cooperative Research Centre for Landscape Environments and Mineral Exploration (CRC LEME). The atlas provides a broad overview of a wide variety of in situ and transported regolith located across South Australia, which have formed from rocks of possible Archean to Quaternary age. The atlas also includes regolith examples from adjacent states. It illustrates the composition, fabric, structure and stratigraphy – where applicable – of dominantly in situ regolith, as well as cases of regolith with mixed origin and/or complex overprinting. The atlas aims to be a teaching, guidance and look-up tool for geologists, explorers and other parties interested in regolith, but is far from representing all types of regolith materials occurring in SA. Where available, further references and links to publications are provided. The hand specimens are grouped and described – where applicable – by regolith materials grouped according to regolith terminology and classification developed in the CRC LEME (Pain et al., 2007; Pain, 2008). Each hand specimen has been photographed, in some cases multiple times. The regolith material hand specimen collection is physically stored in the South Australia Drill Core Reference Library at the Tonsley Precinct and can be viewed upon request. Some samples shown in this atlas are privately owned and do not form part of the actual specimen collection held at Tonsley. However, they have been included here as they show important types of regolith material found in the State, and hence complement the GSSA collection.

title: RB 2021/00002 High precision CA-TIMS dating of the Hiltaba Suite, Gawler Craton.
notes:

resource_urls: https://demstedpprodaue12.blob.core.windows.net/mesac-public/resources/files/5440480/rb2021_02 High precision CA-TIMS dating of the Hiltaba Suite, Gawler Craton.pdf
abstract: This report provides a summary of high-precision chemical abrasion-isotope dilution-thermal ionisation mass spectrometry (CA-IDTIMS) U-Pb geochronology performed on zircon grains from five samples of Hiltaba Suite granites collected at locations spread across the Gawler Craton.  The oldest samples are from the Burgoyne Batholith, host to the Roxby Downs Granite and Olympic Dam Breccia Complex in the Paleoproterozoic–Mesoproterozoic basement beneath the Stuart Shelf on the eastern side of the Gawler Craton. Sample 2131359 (DDH BRD1) from the Saddle Hill prospect east of Olympic Dam is a biotite granite with an emplacement age of 1592.62 ± 0.52 Ma. West of Olympic Dam, granite from DDH Blanche 1, represented by sample 2111460, was emplaced at 1591.79 ± 0.42 Ma.   Sample 2053554, representing the Hiltaba Suite at Tarcoola in the Central Gawler Gold Province (Ferris and Schwarz 2003) is significantly younger at 1586.49 ± 0.49 Ma, as is the Curramulka Gabbronorite on the Yorke Peninsula (1580.21 ± 0.31 Ma), although the latter lies within the same Olympic Cu-Au Province (Skirrow et al. 2007) extending along the eastern margin of the Gawler Craton.  The westernmost sample 2115491, from the Fowler Domain, is the youngest with an emplacement age of 1579.37 ± 0.73 Ma.  The dates given above demonstrate that magmatism in the Gawler Craton continued for up to 8 million years after eruption of the Gawler Range Volcanics, which occurred c. 1594.5–1586.5 Ma (Jagodzinski et al. in prep).   The spatial distribution of all magmatic ages for the Gawler large igneous province (LIP) suggests that magmatism originated in the Olympic Domain (basement to the Stuart Shelf), then propagated radially outward, a pattern which is suggestive of mantle upwelling, whereby a rising and then flattening outwards plume head provided the heat source for melting of the SCLM (sub-crustal lithospheric mantle) and lower crust.

abstract: The PORT AUGUSTA 1:250,000 mapsheet area covers the north-eastern part of the Eyre Peninsula, the northern Spencer Gulf and the south-western Flinders Ranges, and extends from latitude 32°00'S to 33°00'S and longitude 136°30'S to 138°00'S. The main centres of population are the city of Port Augusta and Iron Knob. Access to the area is via the Port Wakefield (A1), Eyre, Stuart and Lincoln Highways. The region is largely occupied by numerous pastoral leases that are used predominantly for sheep grazing. The Cultana Army Training Area, long held by the Australian Defence Force, occupies the Cultana Inlier and part of the adjacent Simmens Plateau, and is used for driver training, infantry manoeuvre and weapons firing exercises. Access to this area is restricted, requiring negotiation with the Federal Defence Force. Onesteel's Whyalla steelworks is located north of False Bay. Natural vegetation is preserved in the Winninowie, Whyalla and Lake Gilles Conservation Parks. This report consists of a review of the geology and mineral potential of the PORT AUGUSTA area, and is a preliminary study of a current mapping programme to revise and update the PORT AUGUSTA 1:250,000 map sheet. The information in this report is largely drawn from MESA and academic publications, company open file Envelopes of exploration reports, and preliminary field reconnaissance by the author.

name: d20011642
title: RB 2016/00037 Vectorisation of residual gravity and TMI data in the northern Gawler Craton: implications for exploration targeting and GIS analysis.
notes:
Geographic Locality: South Australia
Doc No: RB 2016/00037
abstract: Gravity and reduced-to-pole total magnetic intensity grids over the northern Gawler Craton have been vectorised, generating polygon datasets representing regions of locally anomalous gravity and magnetic intensity. Statistics from potential field grids were embedded into each polygon which enabled calculation of anomaly magnitude. Known IOCG-type deposits were found to be consistently associated with coincident to semicoincident magnetic and gravity anomalies, with residual Bouguer gravity anomaly magnitudes greater than 4.8 milliGals (mGal). Known iron ore deposits were found to be associated with residual TMI anomaly magnitudes greater than 3800 nanoTesla (nT). Analysis of spatial clustering and the identification of outliers using Anselin Local Morans I (ESRI, 2013) has resulted in the delineation of geographic regions across the study area that exhibit either high magnitude clusters or high magnitude outliers, which correspond to known regional geological and metamorphic domains. In the eastern Gawler Craton, high magnitude spatial outliers are of particular interest, as they include a high proportion of currently identified iron oxide – copper–gold (IOCG) deposits and mineral occurrences. Moreover, these spatial outliers appear to lie within the Olympic Domain, possible redefining the extent of the domain. Results from this study suggest additional untested spatially coincident magnetic and gravity anomalies that warrant further investigation.

abstract: Sandstone as a building material was used extensively in Adelaide and regional South Australia from the founding of the colony until the end of World War II.  However, since 1945 the industry has declined steadily, with closure of many quarries, until by the 1980s only a small number were left operating on the fringes of Adelaide. Lately, due to the increased demand in recent times for all types of natural dimension stone, an expert study of the State was seen by the SA Government as necessary to identify and evaluate sandstone resources suitable for supplying domestic markets and meeting a growing international demand.  Local consultancy Olliver Geological Services Pty Ltd was commissioned to undertake the project. In discussions with Messrs A.M. Pain (Principal Geologist, PIRSA) and B.J. Cooper (Chief Project Officer, PIRSA), it was agreed to concentrate investigations on the State's Mid-North, southern Flinders Ranges and Eyre Peninsula, where the task of assessing economic potential for re-opening abandoned quarries or developing new resources would be relatively free of side issues arising from the constraints of any nearby residential development and competing land uses, such as vineyards and hobby farms.  Of the types of natural dimension stone resource sought, priority was given to identifying red stone.  Rock colour was determined by using a Munsell Colour Chart for comparison against fresh surfaces of samples stored in the PIRSA Core Library at Glenside, but the selected hue probably does not represent the full range of colour variations that may be accessible should the previously sampled quarries be re-opened. Six geological reconnaissance trips were completed in the period September 1998 to May 1999.  The fifth trip was a three-day inspection of selected quarries, accompanied by Messrs Pain and Cooper. During these geological investigations of sandstone resources, the following quarries were inspected:  Andamooka Flagstone; Whyalla Red and Whyalla White; Spinifex Bluff; Quorn Town (North and South Quarries); Gladstone (two of four quarries); Warnertown; Spalding (three quarries); Brinkworth; Clare (many quarries); Auburn; Manoora (three of five quarries); and Freestone Hill. Ten previously unrecorded quarries were discovered and documented:  Belmonte; Tregolana; Hookina; Quorn Brown; Tickle Belly Hill; Saltia; Pekina; White Rock; Wirrabara; and Auburn East. Four sites were discovered which have not been mined:  Andamooka Red; Tassie Creek; Red Rock; and Whyalla Red and White. A number of other localities were checked en-route, but proved to have no potential. The establishment of an integrated sandstone mining, processing and marketing enterprise is recommended, preferably at Quorn, using stone from:  Hookina - An international standard red stone, suitable for blocks, tiles, walling and paving.  Quorn Town - Continued use should be encouraged in Port Augusta and Quorn, and it should also be considered for replacement use in Adelaide for Mount Lofty-style sandstone constructions.  A suitable marketing name is required.  Quorn Brown - Suitable for prestigious buildings in the region, with the potential to attract a national market.  A suitable marketing name is required.  Tickle Belly Hill - Particularly useful for large retaining walls and lower courses of large buildings.  Saltia - Matching stone for many buildings in Port Augusta.  Pekina Honey - A high quality stone, different in appearance to the five types of stone listed above.  Whyalla Red and White - Ideal for decorative purposes: tiles, table tops, internal panelling and ornaments. The inclusion of stone from Warnertown and Gladstone, both of which are pleasing aesthetically and are durable sandstones, is also desirable to increase the range of colours and textures available.

abstract: Sulfide and oxide trace element geochemical analyses have been conducted on more than 290 core chip samples collected from stored drill cores of 39 drillholes located across South Australia, as part of a collaborative project being conducted between the Centre for Ore Deposit and Exploration Science (CODES), University of Tasmania, and the Geological Survey of South Australia. The project aim was to analyse the mineral chemistry of pyrite, hematite and magnetite across a range of deposit styles in SA, and determine whether the technique could be used to provide insights into, and vector within, the various mineral systems.  Results suggested that pyrite chemistry can be used to successfully distinguish between IOCG, hydrothermal breccia, MVT and sedimentary copper deposits. However, pyrite trace element compositions from both orogenic gold and Au-magnetite skarn deposits partially overlap with those present in these other deposit styles. Magnetite, although present in fewer of the deposit types compared to pyrite, was nonetheless able to yield compositional data that accurately discriminate between IOCG and Au-magnetite skarn deposits.  A case study was made of six drillholes from the GSSA's Mineral Systems Drilling Program. It was concluded that, based on pyrite geochemistry alone, the area around hole MSDP12 may be considered to have the most prospectivity for economic magmatic-hydrothermal mineralisation.  A further case study was made of seven diamond cored holes from company exploration carried out recently at the Intercept Hill prospect, which is located near the Emmie Bluff IOCG mineral deposit. Trace element analyses of 512 individual crystals derived from 30 drill core samples revealed fascinating and complex sulphide and oxide mineral parageneses. Also, halite-hematite intergrowths were discovered which are presumably Mesoproterozoic in age; this finding is regarded as very significant and highly relevant to the origin of IOCG mineralisation in the Gawler Craton and beyond. Furthermore, the prevalence of gold-rich pyrite over a large area at Intercept Hill (extending for ~3 km between IHAD1 and IHAD5) suggests proximity to a large (potentially world-class) magmatic-hydrothermal system.

title: Cultana Regional 3D Geology
abstract:
The Cultana 3D Geological Model covers an area which includes the Roopena and western half of the Cultana
1:100,000 map sheet areas. The geology of the model area comprises a succession of deformed Palaeoproterozoic
sedimentary and intrusive rocks which are overlain by the Corunna Conglomerate and Mesoproterozoic Gawler Range
Volcanics and intruded by the Hiltaba Suite granites. In the east of the model area the Gawler Craton basement is
overlain by a sequence of Neoproterozoic sediments and volcanics of the Stuart Shelf. These sediments have been
eroded from the uplifted block of the Cultana Inlier, to expose the basement below.

name: rb9700051
title: RB 97/00051 Poona copper mine, Moonta, South Australia - Investigation of alteration mineralogy using short-wave infrared analysis.
notes:
Notes: This report is one of a series issued under the recently completed AMIRA project on improved mineral exploration through the use of portable infrared spectroscopy to define and map alteration minerals associated with major ore systems. At Poona, the authors have been able to define alteration haloes related to emplacement of the ore minerals (defined by the mica phengite) and to weathering of the sulphide ore (defined by the presence of the clay halloysite).  These minerals have a broader distribution than the ore minerals and therefore provide a larger target for exploration drilling in the search for buried orebodies.
Geographic Locality: Yorke Peninsula;Moonta;Wallaroo Beach;Alford alteration zone
Doc No: RB 97/00051
Drillhole: DDH230;DDH231;DDH233;DDH234;DDH235;DDH242a;DDH244;DDH245;MP511 - MP513;MP811
abstract: The Poona Copper Mine on northern Yorke Peninsula, South Australia, was worked from 1988-92 on an extension of the original Poona lode, a narrow, shear-hosted copper sulphide vein deposit in Moonta Porphyry of Mesoproterozoic age.  The orebody is typical of extensive mineralised veins in the Moonta district which were discovered in 1861 and produced for over 60 years to make South Australia a significant world source of copper from the 1860s to 1920s.  The mine was selected for a pilot study in spectral mapping because it represents both a well documented, recently mined deposit from a major historic centre for copper production, and an example of a Proterozoic Fe oxide Cu-Au-REE style of mineralisation of which the world class Olympic Dam deposit is also an example. The study involved analyses of mainly drill hole samples using a portable short wave infrared (SWIR) analyser, PIMA II.  PIMA II is representative of a new generation of portable field instruments.  It provides a rapid, cost-effective means of collecting mineralogical data at a drill or mine site.  In this study, spectra were interpreted to determine which alteration minerals could be identified and whether these could be used to assist exploration for similar ore deposits.  Over 550 samples from 13 drill holes were analysed and 732 spectra were recorded and examined.  Minerals which showed SWIR response included chlorite, muscovite, kaolin, alunite, smectite and tourmaline. Subtle variations in spectra, particularly for chlorite, kaolin and muscovite, were noted and investigated in more detail.  For these minerals, spectral interpretations were supported by other analytical techniques including X-ray diffraction (XRD), microprobe analyses and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The spectral data were useful in mapping both regolith units and alteration mineralogy, with the following minerals identified as having a close association with Cu-Au veins and potentially offering broader targets which could be used to focus exploration drilling: · Halloysite and kaolinite coexist as separate kaolin species at Poona.  The distribution of halloysite is largely constrained to the weathered zone and as a coating on fractures in fresh porphyry to depths of around 80 m.  It is argued that at Poona, halloysite is preferentially precipitated from circulating meteoric water high in dissolved aluminium and silica that formed  during acidic conditions resulting from weathering of sulphide ore.  A method of distinguishing halloysite from kaolinite is proposed based on a ratio of the depth of the water feature at 1900 nm and the sum of the depths of the main kaolin absorption features.  Halloysite is distributed as a broad envelope about the orebody and could be targeted in exploration drilling as an indicator to mineralised veins which extend into the weathered zone; · For muscovite, a wavelength shift of the major absorption feature from 2208 nm to 2227 nm is due to a compositional change resulting from substitution of Al by Fe and Mg to approach a phengite composition.  The longer wavelength phengitic micas are particularly well developed in the wallrock immediately adjacent to the ore zone.  Phengitic mica at Poona is interpreted as the result of hydrothermal alteration by fluids associated with sulphide deposition.  Although the phengite zone is typically less than 10 m wide on either side of the orebody, the presence of subparallel shearing with associated minor copper mineralisation extended this zone to 50 m in one drill hole. Broader alteration zones might be expected for larger mineralised veins or for vein stockworks; · Variation in the positions of the chlorite absorption features were due largely to alteration of Fe-rich chlorite with varying proportions of Fe replaced by Mg.  This later stage alteration in chlorite may correspond with the period of ore formation at Poona.  However, the patchy nature of the alteration in individual chlorite grains made it difficult to interpret and map from spectral data alone.  Overall, the interpreted distribution of chlorite with higher Mg content is more restricted than that of Fe-chlorite and appears to be related spatially to the zone of mineralisation.  The presence and composition of chlorite may have more significance in a regional context in identifying areas of metamorphic/metasomatic alteration that favour mobilisation and concentration of Fe-Cu-Au mineralisation.

abstract: This report presents the results of a study jointly conducted by the Geological Survey of South Australia and CSIRO Mineral Resources which aimed to enhance the expression of geological structure in geophysical images and to derive depth to magnetic source estimates over Region 3A of the Gawler Craton Airborne Survey; viz. all of the ANDAMOOKA 1:250k map sheet area. The study was based on magnetic field data acquired during February-June 2017 by this airborne magnetic and radiometric survey commissioned by the Geological Survey of South Australia, that have been combined with ground gravity data from the South Australian state gravity database.  The 2017-18 PACE Copper Gawler Craton Airborne Survey (GCAS) provides both higher resolution and more consistent mapping of the magnetic field than are available from previous coverage by multiple geophysical surveys of lesser extent. Advantages of the new survey data are quite evident upon inspection of the primary total magnetic intensity (TMI) data, but it is through the enhancement of that TMI data to assist in recovery of geological information that the advantages are most clearly expressed.  Many of the enhancements presented in this report are necessarily of limited application to the TMI data previously obtained across the Gawler Craton area, mainly because of known numerous insufficiencies and imperfections in those data, and they would be hampered by the unavoidable effects of abrupt signal strength contrast that appear on passing between survey datasets acquired on different line spacings, flying heights or flight-line orientations. The GCAS data acquisition consistency and close line spacing therefore support higher resolution and more confident source depth mapping from the magnetic field data.  Local magnetic field variations arise exclusively from ferromagnetic minerals which may only constitute of the order of 2% or less of the rock (even for what are considered strongly magnetised rocks), while lateral variations in geology which have no associated variation in magnetisation have no direct expression in the magnetic field imagery. In contrast, gravity data respond to variations in density, to which all components of the rock contribute. Gravity field variations therefore provide a complementary mapping of geology. Suitable combinations and contrasts of gravity and magnetic fields provide more diagnostic information about the subsurface than does the sum of the two fields processed and imaged independently.  The output of this study is a collection of images and digital data products, downloadable herein, which have been  generated to facilitate geological interpretation. The products are not themselves interpretive, but provide more direct access to interpretation than do directly measured datasets treated alone. These products, and in particular the magnetic source depth estimates, are designed to provide the genesis of a ‘live’ resource which can be progressively upgraded rather than simply being replaced when further studies are undertaken in the area, the depth solution database is added to, or when new drillhole information is reported.

name: rb8200090
title: RB 82/00090 Stratigraphic and tectonic significance of South Australian Proterozoic basins.
notes:
Geographic Locality: South Australia
Doc No: RB 82/00090
abstract: This report forms contribution to the working group on Australian Proterozoic basins. The best dated early Proterozoic sequence is the Hutchison Group of the Gawler Craton. Metasediments of the Willyama Complex are correlated with this group and an extensive depositional shelf has been inferred. Other probable early Proterozoic sequences are the Musgrave - Mann Metamorphics, Peake Metamorphics, Radium Creek Metamorphics, Wilgena Hill Jaspilite and Barossa Complex. Early - Middle Proterozoic sequences were deposited in fault troughs accompanied by volcanism. These include McGregor Volcanics, Moonabie Formation, volcanics and breccias of the Olympic Dam deposit, Gawler Range Volcanics, Corunna Conglomerate, Tarcoola Beds and Pandurra Formation. In middle to late Proterozoic, deposition took place in the Adelaide Geosyncline, Officer Basin, Stuart Shelf and Curnamona Cratonic Nucleus.

abstract: Cambrian sediments in the Arrowie Basin were deposited on a rifted continental margin.  Four distinct depositional regimes, ranging from a western, tectonically stable shelf, through platform-ramp to eastern slope and trough-synclines, can be delineated.  Three stratigraphic sequence sets have been defined: the earliest set includes five unconformity-bounded sedimentary sequences, described below in order of their deposition. The lowest sequence 1.0 contains a deltaic-shallow marine succession (Uratanna Formation) which was deposited in depressions and valleys or channels cut into the Ediacara fauna-bearing Rawnsley Quartzite.  The sequence consists of lowstand wedge and submarine channel deposits, transgressive prodelta siltstones, and highstand delta front and shoreface siltstones and sandstones.  This sequence is considered to have been deposited in the same tectonic setting as the underlying Wilpena Group during a major second-order Neoproterozoic sea-level fall, even though the sediments contain Cambrian trace fossils.  A disconformity or major erosion surface which developed between sequence 1.0 and overlying sequences was probably related to a tectonic shift, from the Petermann Ranges Orogeny-related uplift to rifting during the Early Cambrian, which also resulted in a provenance change from the western Gawler Craton to eastern Curnamona Province.  The first Cambrian transgression reached maximum extent during deposition of the uppermost Parachilna Formation and lower Woodendinna Dolomite or equivalents. Subsequent sequence 1.1 sedimentation was interrupted by an intra-shelf regressive event.  This event and its depositional unconformity divide the sequence into two sub-sequences, but the unconformity does not extend beyond the shelf.  Sub-sequence 1.1A (~Tommotian) contains the lowstand to transgressive Parachilna Formation and highstand Woodendinna Dolomite or equivalents, whereas sub-sequence 1.1B (~Atdabanian) is a shelf limestone succession, containing the earliest archaeocyaths and trilobites in Australia.  Sequence 1.2 (~early Botoman) is bounded at the base by the Flinders Unconformity.  Extensional faulting during deposition resulted in carbonate platform shedding and slope sedimentation (e.g. Mernmerna Formation). Sequence 1.3 (late Botoman) sediments were mainly deposited during a relative sea-level fall in subsiding troughs and grabens, and comprise both siliciclastics and carbonates. Sequence set 2 includes siliciclastics or redbeds (Billy Creek Formation) and carbonate (Wirrealpa Limestone), while sequence set 3 includes the Lake Frome Group, mainly red-brown siltstone and sandstone. The latter two sets contain shallow water and deltaic deposits. Sequence 1.3 contains organic-rich shale (Oraparinna Shale, up to 1.43% TOC) and a highstand built, porous archaeocyathan reef complex in the Moorowie Syncline.  The seismic sequence stacking interpretation indicates that possible reefal structures will progradationally overlie the shales in the ramp-slope regions during a sealevel fall, while on the other hand, such structures will also later be overlain by anhydrite and thick siltstone units (potential hydrocarbon seal and source rocks). Pre-sequence 1.3 sediments also contain vuggy reef carbonates and porous sandstones, some of which were deposited in subsurface channel-like structures and have the potential to form hydrocarbon traps. Sequence sets 2 and 3 contain several porous sandstone beds and could be potential petroleum reservoirs.  In drillhole Moorowie 1, good quality oil source rocks occur in the Moodlatana Formation and Wirrealpa Limestone.  Major tectonic uplifting and thermal events during the Early Permian may have matured these Cambrian rocks for oil generation.  In the Moorowie Syncline, faulted-high or 'channel' plays may form prospective petroleum targets.
