abstract: An strong total count radiometric anomaly (to 10 x background), encountered by Minad on the shore of Lake Torrens about 20 miles south-east of Andamooka during aerial reconnaissance surveying, was investigated by drilling 3 shallow vertical open percussion holes over the site of maximum radioactivity during August 1972. Prior to doing the drilling, ground examination of this anomaly had shown that it is associated with localised limonitic infillings to certain parts of a system of joints occurring on a wave cut platform in sandstone exposed at the lake shore. Off-scale (>10,000 counts per second) scintillometer readings were obtained there, during ground traverses made across a total area of about 1600 square yards. by contrast, the background level radiation reading over the sandstone was only 20 cps. Recent analyses of the radioactive limonitic material from the joints had confirmed the high gamma ray radiation count, but neither uranium or thorium could be detected in anomalous amounts. It was subsequently established that the gamma ray emission is almost certainly due to radon 222, this very short-lived radionuclide being produced by radium 226 contained in the ferruginous crust, which has been deposited there by groundwater through geochemical scavenging. It was thought that the parent uranium occurrence from which the radium is derived could possibly exist as a nearby, highly concentrated source.  The three drillholes, with an aggregate penetration of 690 feet, were geologically logged in detail at 5 foot depth intervals, and were geophysically wireline logged with gross gamma, electrical resistivity and spontaneous potential tools. In addition to the intense near-surface radioactivity, a wireline gamma ray log anomaly peaking at 205 cps over 2 feet was detected in the first completed hole AIX1, within a sandstone gravel zone intersected from 42-52 feet depth, while hole AIX3 was being drilled 135 feet away to the north, also on the wave cut platform. However, this log anomaly later disappeared when AIX1 was re-logged in two runs respectively carried out 24 and 48 hours after the completion of AIX3.  It is believed that the variable anomaly observed in the aquifer interval in hole AIX1 resulted from a drilling-induced change in radon gas migration through or into that zone, caused by the pumping of groundwater during the drilling of AIX3. This implies that a second source of radon exists in the area, apart from the radium-rich limonite cement formed at the surface, and also that it must lie close to hole AIX1, since the 3 to 4 day half-life of radon gas allows little time for migration. It is inferred that this new source is most likely to be uranium, present in an as yet unidentified body lying close to the subsurface aquifer interval cut by hole AIX1, which is still shedding both radium and radon gas into this aquifer.  It is concluded that additional drilling is warranted close to hole AIX1, preferably along a north-south traverse parallel to weakly defined local aerial photo lineaments.

abstract: Interest was centred on the Whyalla Sandstone - Pandurra Formation stratigraphic contact (the locus of the Gunyah Lake mineral occurrence), and on a quartzite unit developed adjacent to the Woocalla Dolomite Member (the locus of the House and Main Open Cut orebodies), for the several purposes of further defining and then sampling continuations to known mineralisation, for conducting stratigraphic investigations, and to explore these settings for new copper deposits. The work included undertaking stratigraphic field mapping of sand-covered portions of the licence at scales of 1:5000, 1:10,000 and 1:17,000, supported by stratigraphic drilling traverses (about 550 percussion holes totalling 5500 m), doing extensive geochemical sampling of lake muds in formerly unexplored lagoonal areas, conducting near-mine drilling at Mount Gunson mine, and making IP and EM surveys over resultant downhole geochemical anomalies.  The stratigraphic drilling was highly successful, as it intersected significant new copper sulphide mineralisation at Cattlegrid in January 1972, where follow-up drilling confirmed the economic importance of the discovery.

abstract: Ongoing exploration for a possible Cattlegrid type stratabound copper deposit over an area south-west of Lake Torrens included aerial magnetic and EM surveys, drill testing of EM anomalies by 47 percussion holes totalling 2086 m, a regional magnetic interpretation, detailed petrological and stratigraphic studies, ground magnetic and resistivity surveys (which also aimed to further delineate buried ?Tertiary palaeochannels near Pandurra Homestead), and the preparation of bedrock unit stratigraphic sequence / mineralisation cross sections and 1:50,000 scale lithostratigraphy interpretative maps. The petrography of 7 possible geosynclinal equivalents to the Mount Gunson shelfal rocks were examined (Sturt Tillite - Elizabeth Conglomerate; Tapley Hill Formation - Woocalla Dolomite; Tapley Hill Formation; Seacliff Sandstone - Whyalla Sandstone; Reynella Sandstone - Yudnapinna Siltstone; Brachina Formation - Tregolana Shale). A review of the igneous rocks occurring in the Pandurra area suggested that they are part of a Roopena Volcanics assemblage of mainly tholeiitic basic to intermediate extrusives (but with some late stage acid differentiates), as deduced from their intimate relationships and some recognised affinities with rock types from drillhole Roopena 1. This was a significant revision of the earlier company and government mappers' view at the time, which held that volcanic outcrop and subcrop on the western side of the EL 186 area, between Cariewerloo and Roopena homesteads, was the acidic Gawler Range Volcanics. Sample lithologies identified include basalt, andesite, trachyandesite, trachyte, rhyodacite, rhyolite and tuffaceous rhyolite. Small residual gravity anomalies were thought to be most likely related to intrusives and volcanic flows, and not to the Pandurra Formation. No structures of economic interest were defined.

abstract: Ongoing appraisal work conducted by CSR at the company's newly discovered Cattlegrid copper deposit that lies at the top of the Pandurra Formation has included infill rotary percussion and diamond drilling (13 holes for 554 m, including 166 m cored), ore sampling for petrographic/mineragraphic studies and metallurgical testing, the acquisition of orientation geophysical surveys (including the flying of 260 line km of INPUT aerial EM coverage at 200/400 m line spacing and 130 m mean terrain clearance), and lead isotopic age dating of the ore.  Diamond drillhole LY2 (TD 667.40 m) was drilled vertically through the Cattlegrid orebody, which was shown to be only about 5 m thick below 29.4 m hole depth, although minor sulphide in fractures persists down to 123 m and also occurs in a brecciated zone at the depth interval 144-163 m. A second diamond drillhole, LY3 (TD 246 m), was drilled on a magnetic anomaly located 1 km north-east of Cattlegrid. It encountered copper mineralisation in the Woocalla Dolomite, and then passed into a system of basic dykes that are intruded into the Pandurra Formation. Two stages of basalt-dolerite intrusion can be seen in the drill core, an earlier carbonate-veined stage and a later magnetite-veined stage. This hole was ended prematurely in altered acid volcanic rocks (?Gawler Range Volcanics).  Evaluation of the geophysical test data acquired at Cattlegrid showed that INPUT EM was the most responsive reconnaissance method, being able to define the resistive subcrop edge of the Tregolana Shale Member, and to outline shallow depositional troughs developed on the top of Pandurra unconformity surface. Some good to moderate IP frequency responses were obtained over the Cattlegrid orebody, but ground magnetic, SP and VHEM methods proved unresponsive. The hammer seismic refraction technique was found to be effective in detecting the buried Pandurra unconformity where it lies at depths of down to 30 m.  A tentative age of 1350-920 Ma for the lead (and copper?) mineralisation at Cattlegrid was determined, with an ore remobilisation date of 950-500 Ma.   Brownfields exploration undertaken by CSR to look for repetitions of Cattlegrid type stratiform copper mineralisation included the conduct and interpretation of 2435 line km of detailed aerial EM (INPUT) and aerial magnetic surveys during 1975, and regional stratigraphic drilling (191 rotary percussion holes for 5208 m) which targeted the Whyalla Sandstone / Pandurra Formation stratigraphic contact.  Follow-up of selected IP and INPUT EM anomalies by rotary percussion/diamond core drilling on a 200 m grid (15 holes for 605 m, including 281 m of core) led to the discovery and delineation of the MG14 deposit (800,000 tonnes averaging 1.98% Cu over 3 m) under 20-25 m of cover 1 km north of Cattlegrid, which is thought to have formed within a channel-filling, dolomitic, laminated dark clay facies deposited near the top of the Woocalla Dolomite.  Similar (>1% Cu) thin mineralised channel intercepts were also later found by drilling 16 rotary percussion/diamond core holes for 553 m (396 m cored) in the Gully area adjacent to the abandoned Main Open Cut; by drilling 20 RC holes for 690 m near the LY3 drillhole; and in drillhole MG41.

abstract: Extensive geochemical and geological investigations were carried out over exposed and shallowly buried, predominantly flat-lying Lower Cambrian carbonate rocks in an area extending from the western edge of the Flinders Ranges to west of Lake Torrens.  It was considered that lead-zinc mineralisation revealed by the South Australian Department of Mines' exploration in the basal Cambrian dolomites of the Ediacara structure, although sub-economic, was significant.  In a broader sense, it was also realised that much more extensive nearby occurrences of Lower Cambrian carbonate rocks had not been systematically explored for base metal mineralisation.  The concept behind this search aim was that, at Ediacara, the mode of occurrence of base metals in small and discontinuous orebodies, concentrated at levels between 100 and 200 feet above the Cambrian - Precambrian contact, is suggestive of some broad stratigraphic control to such mineral emplacement.  The resulting work programmed involved performing detailed stream sediment and rock chip sampling, reconnaissance IP and ground magnetic surveying, diamond drilling of drainage lead anomalies and pseudo-gossanous Fe-Mn enriched outcrops recognised near the north-western margin of Lake Torrens (3 holes, total 642 feet) and near Brachina Gorge (5 holes, total 2525 feet), and geological mapping and petrographic studies of lead-mineralised horizons that were found within a 20 mile-long zone at the western edge of the central Flinders Ranges between Bunyeroo Gorge and Parachilna Gorge.  The conclusion was that lead-zinc sulphide mineralisation, although undoubtedly extensive in the stratigraphic setting envisaged, was persistently feeble, with no plausible indications of economic metal concentrations, nor clues as to the direction in which such concentrations could be expected.

name: mesac31454
title: Classification of igneous rocks from the Pandurra area.
abstract: Apart from doleritic intrusive igneous rocks and some sediments, all of the fine-grained igneous rocks examined are thought to be part of a Roopena Volcanics assemblage of mainly tholeiitic basic to intermediate extrusive rocks (but with some late stage acid differentiates), as deduced from their intimate relationships and some recognised affinities with rock types from SADM Roopena DDH1. This is a significant revision of the earlier company and government mappers' view which held that volcanic outcrop and subcrop on the western side of the EL 186 area between Cariewerloo and Roopena homesteads was the acidic Gawler Range Volcanics.  Sample lithologies now identified include basalt, andesite, trachyandesite, trachyte, rhyodacite, rhyolite and tuffaceous rhyolite.  These are now redefined as belonging to the Roopena Volcanics suite, a rock association overlying the Gawler Craton which forms the basal unit of the Adelaidean sequence on the Stuart Shelf.

abstract: Exploration conducted by CSR Ltd for possible economic stratiform base metal deposits in the western part of EL 81 addressed several targets, including Cattle Grid type disconformity - related copper mineralisation, Sweet Nell / MG14 type dolomite-hosted mineralisation, lead-zinc mineralisation in black shales, and mineralisation associated with basic dykes and faults.  The Lake Macfarlane south-western region of the tenement is now being relinquished because it is considered to have a low exploration potential for copper and other base metals. Thirteen widely spaced scout rotary percussion holes were drilled in the vicinity of this salt lake, with all terminating in Pandurra Formation or younger rocks.  Only two of these holes were drilled within the now relinquished area (total penetration 138 m), but no significant mineralisation was intersected.

title: Data release [made at SA Director of Mines' discretion] : Andamooka (part of the Stuart Shelf Project). Progress reports to licence expiry/renewal, for the period 2/5/1975 to 1/5/1977. [ Index Part 1 of 2 ].
notes:
Notes: This release to the public of the subject mineral exploration data, namely, company data which was acquired more than 5 years ago, is being done by DMITRE in accord with the provisions of Section 77D of the Mining Act 1971 and Regulation 88 of the Mining Regulations 2011. Data from this tenement is part of the fourth public release of historic information pertaining to a number of formerly confidential WMC Stuart Shelf licences.  The index has been separated into two logical parts to accomodate the extent of subject matter summary description required to allow concise reference retrieval.   WMC's first public announcement about the discovery of the giant Olympic Dam copper deposit was made at its AGM held on 18/11/1976. The orebody was found by diamond drillhole RD1 drilled on EL 190 during July 1975, with significant copper suphides (chalcocite) first recognised during a delayed inspection of that hole's retrieved drillcore during September 1975. The size of the discovery was confirmed by drillhole RD10 during early November 1976, when it encountered mineralisation grading an average 2.12% Cu over a 170 m thick cored interval within highly altered and iron-enriched pre-Adelaidean acid igneous basement rocks. After WMC had made this initial press release, the later-detected substantial uranium content of these same rocks cored by RD10 (averaging 0.58 kg/t U3O8 over 170 m) was announced in the company's next quarterly report, made public on 11/2/1977.   Ministerial consent was granted on 1/3/1977 to an agreement for amalgamated licence expenditure commitments on WMC's Stuart Shelf ELs 190, 231, 232, 233, 269, 279, 292, 293 and 294.  Tenure over the same area has subsequently been re-issued to WMC as EL 344.  Includes:   - Milton, B.E., 13/8/1975. Summary of seismic experiments [conducted] on EL 190 during May 1975 (South Australia Department of Mines contractor's report for WMC -  unpublished Report Book 790 [confidential series]; 15 pages, 6 fig, 1 ref).

abstract: An inaugural exploration licence covering land in the Roxby Downs Station and Andamooka Station holdings was taken up by Western Mining Corp. (WMC) to document the stratigraphic section present in the northern portion of the Stuart Shelf tectonic region, and to investigate the base metal potential of largely flat-lying Cambrian and Precambrian metasediments believed to be present in the subsurface on this previously unexplored ground. It was intended to undertake geophysical surveys and drilling, to gather information intended primarily to ascertain whether suitable environments exist there for the formation of economic stratiform copper deposits, perhaps of the Mount Gunson / Cattle Grid deposit style, which is spatially associated with the Proterozoic Pandurra Formation -  Whyalla Sandstone unconformity.  At the outset of exploration field work, a refraction/reflection seismic survey was conducted by WMC near Olympic Dam [i.e. the original water storage geographical feature] on Roxby Downs Station during May 1975, to help define the likely depth to top of pre-Adelaidean basement, and thus constrain the depth required to be attained in test stratigraphic drilling. Two refraction lines, one north-south 5 km long, the other east-west 6.5 km long, plus a 1 line km continuous reflection profile, were shot and recorded in the vicinity of this particular dam by contractor the South Australian Department of Mines (SADM). The survey results were interpreted by the Department's Chief Geophysicist, Mr B.E. Milton (cf. RB 790). The survey proved to be a technical success, by clearly demonstrating the existence of seismic velocity contrasts in the Marinoan quartzites, sandstones and shales of the Tent Hill Formation, while the continuous reflection profile laid out east of the dam defined a possible basement reflective seismic event at ~291 +/- 34 m vertical depth. In addition to the seismic survey work, one 24 km long ground magnetic traverse that passed directly through the Olympic Dam locality was acquired along 321.5 degrees True direction, to provide detailed magnetic data to enable a calculation of depth to the top of a magnetic anomaly interpreted as originating from basement rocks. However, the resulting ground magnetic data yielded a profile that was almost identical to that produced by earlier BMR 4-mile regional airborne magnetic data. This similarity was interpreted as indicating that the source of the magnetic anomaly lay at considerable depth, i.e. within ?Cleve Metamorphics crystalline basement. 7 vertical percussion holes with a total penetration of 330 m were drilled by WMC during July 1975, in a search for groundwater which it was hoped could supply both its planned diamond drilling project and Roxby Downs Station needs. Only hole RDP1 found water, but of a quantity insufficient to provide drilling requirements for exploratory hole RDD1 then already underway.   During June-July 1975, vertical stratigraphic diamond drillhole RDD1 was completed at the Roxby Downs prospect to a total depth of 411 m, from a site 400 m west of Olympic Dam, to test a coincident magnetic and gravity high that was inferred to represent a geophysical response of a kind that could be caused by buried basic volcanic rocks (possibly Roopena Volcanics). After passing through the Stuart Shelf Cambrian and Adelaidean metasedimentary cover sequence comprising (from the surface downwards) Andamooka Limestone, Arcoona Quartzite, Corraberra Sandstone and Woomera / Tregolana Shale, probable basement was reached at 335.73 m depth, when the hole passed from a very thin layer of medium grained red sandstone with heavy mineral cross-bedding into what appeared to be a coarse grained, red haematitic amygdaloidal basic volcanic rock. The NQ/BQ drill core was chip sampled at nominal 2 m intervals during early August, and these samples were sent for laboratory assaying to determine the diagnostic trace metal contents of the strata encountered. Significant copper mineralisation was reported in the assay results from sampling of the bottommost unit drilled, together with elevated gold and silver, e.g. 1.02% Cu, 0.29 ppm Au and 3.7 ppm Ag on average over the depth interval 353-391 m, with higher grade thick (to 18 m) zonal intercepts within this interval variously attaining maximum values of 1.32% Cu, 0.45 ppm Au and 5.1 ppm Ag. In view of these good results, the RDD1 diamond core was resampled using half-core splits to get a more representative assay; this yielded average values of 1.047% Cu, 91 ppm Mo, 11.34% Fe and 4.0 ppm Ag over the same depth interval 353-391 m, including peak values of 1.382% Cu, 145 ppm Mo and 5.9 ppm Ag over the interval 359-367 m. The stratigraphy of RDD1 was re-interpreted following receipt of the drill core assay results, to have ?Whyalla Sandstone as the very thin sandy horizon unconformably overlying ?Pandurra Formation at 335.73 m depth, and the core recovered from below this depth was re-logged to produce a different geological description of the mineralised ?Pandurra unit, viz. "red altered fragmental rock composed of angular quartz fragments set in a sericite-quartz-haematite matrix". The host material composition was studied via X ray diffraction determination of its mineralogy, and rock bulk density measurements were made.  During late August 1975, vertical stratigraphic diamond drillhole RDD2 was completed by WMC at the Roxby Downs South prospect to a total depth of 513 m, from a site ~2 km east of Appendicitis Dam, to test a coincident magnetic and gravity high that was inferred to underlie a similar but more shallowly lying stratigraphic section than had been encountered in RDD1. Due to the copper discovery made in that particular hole, the target for RDD2 was to intersect stratiform copper mineralisation formed in a comparable setting above probable, but as yet not found, altered basic volcanic rocks [to accord with Douglas Haynes' original metallogenetic model for Stuart Shelf copper mineralisation, which was adopted in 1972 by WMC]. The hole was percussion precollared to 120 m depth, and then diamond cored through the Stuart Shelf Adelaidean strata until reaching an unconformity at 437 m depth, whereupon the hole passed from quartzite into a thin horizon of dolomite. This in turn was underlain with sharp  unconformity at 439.64 m by non-magnetic ?Pandurra Formation red-bed shales, gritty sandstones and conglomerates commonly showing heavy mineral banding. No copper mineralisation was seen, and no assay values of note were returned from drill core sampling done at 2 m intervals.  The third quarter of tenure of EL 190 was partly devoted to obtaining improved geophysical coverage in the Roxby Downs prospect area. A three-line prospect grid totalling 70 km was laid out and levelled around a baseline connecting drillholes RDD1 and RDD2. Then a seismic refraction survey was  shot during November 1975, recording 40.94 line km of spread along two of the transverse grid lines. Following this, ground magnetic and gravity surveys were read over the grid during December 1975, with coinciding readings taken at 90 m station spacings. This detailed gravity data permitted more precise definition of the amplitude of the Roxby Downs gravity anomaly (20 mGal, compared to the 8 mGal that was estimated from the former regional gravity data acquired at 4 mile spacing by the SADM). In addition, downhole geophysical logging was performed on 30/10/1975 through the entirety of the two open diamond drillholes by contractor SADM, with gamma ray and neutron tools being run to confirm the anomalous subsurface radioactivity which WMC had earlier detected, when it had gamma ray logged hole RDD1 during September with its own wireline tool. A planned programme of selective diamond drilling to define the extent and strength of copper mineralisation discovered by RDD1 was begun in mid-December 1975, initially via percussion precollaring of a pattern of ten vertical holes (RP8 - RP15, plus RP 17 and RP18, for 865 m) centred on that location. An addition percussion hole, RP16, was drilled to 50 m depth at Sunday Well in an unsuccessful search for potable and/or drilling supply groundwater. Two diamond cored holes, RD3 and RD4, were next completed for a total penetration of 734.35 m (561.5 m cored). RD3 was sited 400 m south-east of RDD1, while RD4 was sited 400 m north-west of it. No definite Pandurra Formation was intersected below the Woomera / Tregolana Shale horizon in either case. Both holes were terminated within granite basement, which gave disappointing copper assays (2 m @ 0.57% Cu in RD3, and a maximum of only 0.123% Cu in RD4), and had undetectable levels of uranium. Also during this quarter, the results of assaying the RDD1 drill core for uranium were received, for rocks penetrated below 335 m depth: an average uranium content of 72 ppm (0.16 lb/ton) U was measured for the 59 m thick interval 335.87-395.00 m.  During the fourth quarter of licence Year 1, diamond drillhole RD5, located about 1 km north of RDD1, was completed to a total depth of 461.66 m, but was terminated prematurely due to difficult drilling conditions. The hole entered pre-?Pandurra Formation altered granite basement at 325.74 m depth, and therein found a thick occurrence of chalcocite-haematite mineralisation that provided a much-needed stimulus for WMC's exploration effort. Assaying of the split drill core returned 96 m @ 1.00% Cu and 3.8 ppm Ag from the depth interval 364-460 m, including 34 m @ 1.25% Cu and 3.8 ppm Ag from 364-398 m. Uranium assay values were low (40-60 ppm U). No significant values were obtained for Ni, Co, Mn, Mo, Pb, Zn, Sn or Au. The iron content of the entire copper-mineralised basement intercept (which remained open-ended at the hole's TD) averaged 4.08% Fe. Diamond drillhole RD6 was also started in this period, from a site located 400 m north-east of RDD1, and at 2/5/1976 was at 403 m depth. It encountered some basic or andesitic volcanic rocks interlayered with fragmental haematitic units, immediately beneath the Woomera (Tregolana) Shale, between 326.48 and 354.14 m depth. These volcanic rocks were the first such encountered by WMC's drilling, and were found to contain slightly anomalous Ni, Co, Cu, Pb and Zn. In further geophysical work, data were interpreted for the seismic refraction profiles that had been acquired during the previous quarter in an attempt to follow laterally the seismic break the SADM had detected at Olympic Dam, which WMC formerly had thought must originate from the basement rocks. However, the new seismic data made it apparent that this particular event is caused by the unconformity between the Pandurra Formation and the Woomera Shale.

abstract: At the commencement of the term of the subject licence, exploratory/appraisal diamond drilling using a single rig was continued on the Olympic Dam gravity anomaly by the licensee for gathering more geological information to use to try to understand the mineralisation style of the newly discovered copper-gold-uranium deposit. Six vertical, percussion precollared holes (RD14 - RD19) were completed and geophysically logged with a downhole gamma ray, SP and resistivity probe, and the recovered drill cores were geologically logged, assayed and sampled for bulk magnetic susceptibility and specific gravity of the basement rocks.  Hole RD16 was unusual in that it encountered minor acid to intermediate volcanic rock strata interbedded with sediments which had been incorporated into the granite breccia. Hole RD 19 was also notable for containing a discrete zone of copper and gold mineralisation within otherwise barren breccias, viz. 13 m @ 2.0% Cu, 15.4 g/t Au and 34 ppm U3O8 from 422-435 m depth. This zone is unlike other mineralised zones previously encountered at Olympic Dam, in that it consists almost entirely of chalcocite and is very rich in gold but poor in uranium. After all of the preliminary diamond core geological studies were finished in February 1978, WMC was of the opinion that the Olympic Dam mineralisation appeared to be preferentially associated with the sediment-rich polymictic breccias. By early 1978, the results became available of a test IP-resistivity survey performed in February 1977, when 4.6 line km of frequency domain IP data had been gathered over the orebody using a 100 m spaced dipole-dipole array, and 7 resistivity depth soundings had been  made. Apparent resistivities are generally in the range 50-100 ohm-m in the vicinity of the gravity anomaly, and drop sharply on the eastern flank to around 20-30 ohm-m.  No IP anomalies were recorded. In addition, the geochemical data from a detailed, 548 sample minus 80 mesh size fraction, 100 m x 200 m and 100 m x 100 m soil survey of the prospect grid completed during August 1977 was interpreted. No trace metal leakage through deep cover over the deposit could be detected. During May-June 1978, a ground magnetic survey was conducted to the north of the prospect grid at Olympic Dam, to detail the northern flank of the magnetic anomaly. As well, separate  experimental time domain induced polarization and resistivity investigations were undertaken by the South Australian Department of Mines and Energy over the Olympic Dam copper deposit, but were unable to directly detect the mineralisation (see RB 78/133).  Deep diamond drilling was resumed in July 1978 with two more powerful rigs than had been used previously, in order to penetrate further down into the deposit. Hole RD16, located 400 m east of the discovery hole RD7, and situated near the centre of the geophysically mapped Olympic Dam structure, was deepened from its earlier TD at 419.7 m to 1318.9 m, as RD16a. Caving in this hole from 480 m depth necessitated wedging off at 445 m depth, and a reduction in bore diameter to AQ size. A number of significant thick mineralised intercepts were made in this much extended hole, viz.  458-474 m : 16 m @ 1.36% Cu;  666-732 m : 66 m @ 2.0% Cu + 1.62 lbs/tonne U3O8;  815-868 m : 53 m @ 1.3% Cu + 0.94 lbs/tonne U3O8; and  924-1098 m : 174 m @ 0.37% Cu. Hole RD20, located 1200 m east of RD16, and situated near the eastern edge of the geophysically mapped Olympic Dam structure, was deepened from its earlier TD at 465.9 m to 830.65 m, as RD20a. Here too a number of very significant mineralised intercepts were made, viz.  369-450 m : 81 m @ 1.0% Cu + 0.53 lbs/tonne U3O8;  450-580 m : 130 m @ 2.8% Cu + 2.43 lbs/tonne U3O8; and  620-650 m : 30 m @ 1.0% Cu + 0.51 lbs/tonne U3O8. RD20a was still intersecting economic grades of copper mineralisation when drilling was stopped at 830 m depth. This mineralisation was predominantly chalcopyrite-bornite-magnetite hosted within thin fine-grained and bedded zones in faulted granite breccias.  By the beginning of November 1978, when the above drill core assay results were to hand, WMC was able to announce at its corporate AGM that its recent deep drilling had added greatly to the known extent of the body of economic copper-uranium mineralisation at Olympic Dam, and had clearly shown that it persists to greater depths than indicated previously, with attendant grades of both copper and uranium which exceed those obtained in earlier drilling of other parts of the prospect. Therefore it was apparent to the company that a major mining and processing operation would inevitably become established in the Roxby Downs region in due course, and it was also evident that the work of exploring the deposit in detail and proving its viability, plus designing and planning the mining and ore processing operation, would amount to a considerable task that then was beyond the company's means. Consequently, WMC entered into discussions with a number of interested parties regarding their possible participation in the ongoing project.  Further experimental IP surveying was carried out over Olympic Dam by WMC during September 1978, using 200 m and 300 m dipole-dipole arrays to profile 4.9 line km along a single prospect grid line passing through RD20. The results suggested a possible chargeability anomaly at depth to the east of RD20, which the company proposed to test with hole RD22. During October 1978, the ground gravity survey coverage at Olympic Dam prospect was extended northwards to match the ground magnetic coverage previously augmented.  Late in October 1978 WMC, with the in-field assistance of SADM personnel, undertook a trial radon detection track etch survey over the Olympic Dam prospect area, deploying 234 cups to collect readings of surface radioactive emanations made during a nominal 30-day period. The results did not indicate any meaningful relationship between the observed low level of radon abundance and the known buried uranium mineralisation.  Early in 1979, WMC performed ground magnetic and gravity surveys over the area situated between the Olympic Dam and Phillips Ridge prospects, and began acquiring similar ground geophysical coverage across the Wirrda Well prospect. Plans were made to acquire airborne magnetic and radiometric data over the subject licence area, as part of a regional detailed survey scheduled to take place starting in September 1979.  A contract was signed with Geosearch Pty Ltd to fly this survey along 400 m spaced lines, using a 100 m sensor flight elevation above ground surface and a 60 m sampling interval.  Stratigraphic/exploratory drilling was resumed during April 1979, when DDH ACD1 was started at Appendicitis [Dam] prospect (later re-named Acropolis prospect) and was drilled to an interim TD of 800 m, whereat the hole was stopped pending its later continuation using a larger depth capacity drill rig. Basement in this hole was reached at 717.8 m depth, and comprises intensely haematite-altered rock containing minor chalcopyrite and exhibiting weak radioactivity. During June 1979 a report was received from a mineralogical consultant who had been retained by WMC to conduct an X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy study of the uranium and rare earth - bearing minerals present in the Olympic Dam deposit. Five polished sections prepared from drill core samples of holes RD10, 11, 14 and 17 had been examined. Uranium minerals identified included the oxides uraninite (black) and nasturan (white), a uranium silicate, coffinite, and a uranium titanate, brannerite. Rare earth - bearing minerals found were an aluminium hydroxy-phosphate, florencite, and a fluoro-carbonate, bastnaesite.  The formal signing of a $60 million, 3-year joint venture agreement between WMC and British Petroleum (BP) was announced to the public on 27/7/1979. The Stuart Shelf JV Project was primarily designed to allow the rapid completion of a mining feasibility study for the Olympic Dam copper-gold-uranium deposit, besides giving BP the option of participating in further exploration to be pursued beyond Olympic Dam. Equity in the project would be WMC 51% and BP 49%, with WMC operating.

abstract: (Abstract continued)  During the fifth quarter of WMC's tenure of EL 190, a programme of stepout appraisal diamond drilling was continued, to assess the size of the copper-uranium occurrence discovered by hole RD1 (previously called RDD1 by WMC). Vertical drillhole RD6, located 400 m north-east of RD1, was completed at a total depth (TD) of  487.0 m on 4/6/1976. Below the basal Adelaidean unconformity reached at 326.48 m depth, a 13 m thick unit of chloritised-carbonated acid volcanic rock (?rhyolite flows) was intersected. Beneath this, from 339.0 m to end-of-hole, a red-bed unit of haematitic conglomerate and massive haematite-rich siltstone occurs. No indications of granite were seen, and thus a fault was invoked to lie between RD6 and RD1. The volcanics were found to contain elevated copper and zinc (Cu to 670 ppm, Zn to 1760 ppm), but the red-beds had only a low trace metal content. Vertical drillhole RD7, located 400 m east-northeast of hole RD5 (in which a 96 m thick copper mineralised zone had recently been found), and therefore situated about 1.6 km north of RD1, was completed at TD 447.0 m on 6/8/1976. Basement consisting of haematitic fragmented granite was reached at 315.68 m depth, passing at 359.7 m into a quartz-haematite breccia which continued to end-of-hole. Only trace copper values, to 170 ppm Cu, were returned from drill core sample assaying. In other work performed at this time, seven more percussion pre-collar holes were drilled as part of the prospect appraisal pattern, and two other percussion holes were drilled to attempt to locate useable groundwater. A single vibroseis seismic reflection traverse of 15 line km was recorded during late June-early July by contractor SSL, along the grid baseline surveyed  between drillholes RD1 and RD2 (previously called RDD2), and the reflector data were processed via 12-fold stack to attempt to define the depth and character of the crystalline basement. The seismic profile obtained was of poor quality and difficult to interpret, but it appeared that the granitic rocks which had been drilled did not exhibit the traits of part of a Carpentarian basement complex.    Vertical diamond drillhole RD8, which was drilled during July-August 1976 at a location 400 m north-northwest of hole RD5 , was completed at TD 600 m on 7/8/1976. Very haematitic fragmented and brecciated granite basement was reached at 334.53 m depth. Assaying of the split drill core showed that significant but sub-economic copper mineralisation (predominantly chalcocite) had been intersected within a 78 m thick zone extending from 348 m to 426 m depth, that included an intercept of 12 m @ 1.11% Cu from 356-368 m, with minor thin and weaker intercepts persisting to below 517 m. Diamond drillhole RD9, located 400 m west-southwest of hole RD5 , was completed at TD 500 m on 30/9/1976. Sericitic-haematitic granite basement was reached at 331.03 m depth. Similar mineralisation to that found in RD8, but slightly more disseminated, was encountered over two broad zones; 50 m @ 0.47% Cu from 386-436 m, and 18 m @ 0.56% Cu from 462-480 m. During the sixth quarter of tenure of EL 190, a much more suitably aligned, surveyed and levelled prospect grid was prepared in the Olympic Dam area, over a total line length of 62 km. This grid was used as the base for a detailed ground gravity survey conducted by WMC during October 1976, with readings taken at 100 m station spacings along the entire grid, aimed at establishing the likely distribution of the massive haematite-bearing rocks which the company had realised are the primary cause of the Roxby Downs gravity anomaly. In addition, downhole gamma ray, resistivity and SP wireline geophysical logs were run in all accessible drillholes on the Roxby Downs prospect.  During the seventh quarter of WMC's tenure of EL 190, ground magnetic surveying was undertaken on the new Roxby Downs prospect grid, to complement the detailed gravity data. The combined results were to be used by WMC to relate the Olympic Dam mineralisation occurrences to anomalous geophysical properties of the basement rocks, with the intent of providing future exploration guidance both locally and regionally in the selection and ranking of other geophysical anomalies as drilling targets.  Vertical diamond drillhole RD10, which was drilled during October-November1976 at a location 400 m south-southwest of hole RD5 in order to test for continuity of mineralisation between RD1 and RD5, was completed at TD 529.0 m on 11/11/1976. Basement consisting of haematitic granite breccia was reached at 325.41 m depth. Below 348 m, this rock contains high grade copper mineralisation extending continuously down to 516 m, i.e. over a 168 m thickness, that comprises chalcocite, bornite and chalcopyrite which drill core sample assaying results received at the end of the following week revealed as having an average copper content of 2.13% Cu.  The uppermost 88 m of the mineralised interval includes zones of 16 m @ 3.42% Cu and 10 m @ 4.38% Cu.  [In view of this exciting and unexpectedly large ore occurrence, and its central relationship to copper grades of >1% discovered in four previous holes at the Roxby Downs prospect, which together span a 1.5 km wide area, WMC decided on 18/11/1976 to make an initial public media announcement regarding its now very promising copper mineral discovery made essentially out of 'blind' target exploration conducted on the company's Stuart Shelf Project. Subsequent to making this telling release, WMC received from Amdel Laboratories the results of separate, still confidential assays made for uranium on the RD10 drill core samples. They revealed that this drillhole had also found a very large body of primary uranium mineralisation of mineable grade, giving an intercept of 170 m @ 0.58 kg/t U3O8 that exactly matched the copper-bearing interval. In view of this physically bound-in uranium situation,the discovery's size and its unavoidable influence on any future development of the Olympic Dam copper deposit, WMC went public with the uranium assay results from RD10 when it made its next company activity quarterly report to the Melbourne Stock Exchange, on 11/2/1977].       During the final, eighth quarter of tenure of EL 190, WMC continued its deposit evaluation drilling with drillholes sited on a closer-spaced grid pattern to block out the expected lateral continuity of the zone of high grade mineralisation. Vertical diamond drillholes RD11, RD12 and RD 13 were put in as part of a 5-hole group pattern around RD10, at an average distance of 150 m away from that hole, to TDs of 732.35 m, 575.02 m and 471.60 m respectively. Further percussion precollar drilling was also carried out, with two holes completed adjacent to RD10 as part of a 100 m x 100 m square grid, and another four holes completed as part of a wider 800 m x 800 m square stepout grid also arranged around RD10. Copper and uranium mineralisation was intersected in all three diamond drillholes, but was of a considerably lower average grade than that found by RD10, although the intercept thicknesses were still very large (aggregating 248 m in RD11). The copper mineral assemblage includes chalcocite, bornite, digenite and chalcopyrite, but the species zonation is very complicated. The entrained uranium minerals, which are very fine grained (1-2 microns), include pitchblende, uraninite and probable davidite. Routine downhole gamma ray logging of each completed diamond drillhole was continued. Metallurgical studies of the mineralisation found in RD10 were commenced.

Low value base metal intersections made from drilling (2 diamond holes, SAU29 and SAU30, total 157.33 m, and 4 percussion holes, PUB52 to PUB55, total 811 m) have led to a downgrading of the prospectivity of the area (although initially, percussion hole PUB52 intersected chalcopyrite grading 4 m @ 5600 ppm Cu, and galena and sphalerite grading 2 m @ 1350 ppm Pb and 5300 ppm Zn, at the base of the Tapley Hill section). abstract: Stratiform copper sulphides, hosted within the basal Tapley Hill Formation, and extensions of known kimberlite bodies were targeted in this program.  Reconnaissance and closer (down to 1 km x 1 km) spaced diamond and percussion drilling (28 and 83 holes respectively, totalling 2272 m of coring and 7657 m of open hole) indicated the presence of modest but regionally widespread concentrations of copper, lead and lesser zinc mineralisation, and the base metal potential of the area is considered to be high, with similarities to the Zambian Copperbelt geological setting and with zoning of metal mineralogy at depth. Groundwater monitoring and sampling were carried out in all drillholes to provide hydrogeological data about standing water levels, well yield and groundwater salinity.

abstract: As part of continuing brownfields exploration for extensions to known stratiform base metal mineralisation in the area lying to the west of Pernatty Lagoon, much stratigraphic drilling (210 rotary percussion holes totalling 12,441 m, including 1167 m of core drilling), plus ground follow-up of results from an aerial EM survey flown in February 1975, have eliminated certain geologically unfavourable areas from the possibility of hosting further Cattlegrid or MG14 type deposits. Other exploratory work done recently has included orientation sampling of mulga and myall tree vegetative parts for biogeochemical surveys at Cattlegrid and MG14, trial resistivity profiling of the top of Pandurra Formation palaeosurface in the Mount Gunson and Oakden Hill areas, interpretation of the February 1975 Winnie Pinnie airborne INPUT EM survey data (2435 line km flown on E-W lines at 400 m line spacing and 120 m flight height), re-interpretation of the INPUT data by amplitude ratio analysis, interpretation of the 1975 Winnie Pinnie survey low level aerial magnetic data, acquisition and interpretation of additional aerial INPUT EM and magnetic surveys over two areas in January 1977, biogeochemistry at New Mosely Dam, mapping of interpreted bedrock lithology, geophysical logging of drillholes from Lake Dutton and Bookaloo prospects, acquiring Crone pulse EM profiles at Cattlegrid and at INPUT anomaly J, and making petrographic studies of the MG14 deposit drill core. Shallow percussion drilling for geochemical samples at Selby Dam delineated 2 minor copper anomalies, and drillhole LW23 at Lake Windabout intersected 3 m grading 0.5% Cu.  Mine exploratory drilling from the floor of the open cut pit (2 inclined diamond holes, total 82.2 m) to look for possible fault-controlled extensions to the Cattlegrid copper deposit failed to disclose additional economic mineralisation.  Another 16 diamond drillholes totalling 456 m (156 m cored) were put down at the MG14 deposit to evaluate the type of copper mineralisation and to obtain bulk metallurgical samples.  Results show that the MG14 deposit contains 860,000 tonnes of ore grading 2.08% Cu, but there are likely to be milling and metal recovery problems.  It appears that when using froth flotation, there are large differences in the copper recovery for ore from different deposits or areas within deposits, but the addition of dispersants may prove helpful in raising recovery above 70%. Again, in the MG14 area it seems that there is little outlying mineralisation, although locally, embayments of Woocalla Dolomite are considered prospective.

abstract: Exploration for possible commercial accumulations of sedimentary shallow marine phosphorite ore in the Ediacara 'Sub-basin', 26 km west of Beltana, has consisted of a search within the Early Cambrian strata for any sites or layers of phosphate enrichment which might point to the existence of such accumulations.  After reviewing past exploration work in the area, which has mainly targeted stratabound base metals, a number of stored previous exploratory drillhole cores were examined and sedimentologically logged, besides which 315 core samples were taken for phosphate analysis.  Only trace to very low phosphate concentrations were detected, most of them occurring within siliceous dolomite breccias of the Ajax Limestone and in weathered shales and siltstones of the Parachilna Formation, the latter occurrences being clearly a product of supergene processes.  The best grade found (2.33% P2O5 in Carpentaria DDH E7) is still far short of the minimum 15% P2O5 required for any mining to be feasible.  As follow-up to this sampling, another 212 core samples were taken for phosphate analysis from other stored drillholes put down elsewhere in the Arrowie Basin, to test unweathered parts of the Andamooka Limestone, a more basinal equivalent of the Ajax Limestone.  All these samples yielded still poorer results, below 0.90% P2O5, so all further work was terminated.

abstract: During a search for possible Stuart Shelf - type Proterozoic or Cambrian stratiform base metal deposits within an area lying to the south of Port Pirie, exploratory percussion drilling of 5 vertical holes totalling 443 m was undertaken.  Three of the drillholes failed to penetrate the thick Cainozoic cover on the Wandearah Plains, while another hole, PWD2,  drilled to TD 116 m in the Barunga Ranges at the south-eastern corner of the licence area, was abandoned after reaching upper Adelaidean Tent Hill Formation.  The target Pandurra Erosional Surface is thus concluded to here lie below the economic depth limit for percussion drilling.  No anomalous base metal values were intersected in any hole.  Hole PWD5, drilled in the northern Barunga Ranges, passed through the Skillogalee Dolomite / Nelshaby Sandstone Member disconformable contact, which may be the possible equivalent of the Pandurra Erosional Surface. This hole was abandoned in fractured quartzite at 97 m depth. A Cambrian basin filled with dense carbonate rock is presently interpreted to lie beneath the Wandearah West geophysical anomaly.  It is now thought that the Cultana Batholith granitic basement rocks do not extend across Spencer Gulf onto the EL 200 area, as had been inferred previously in making regional correlations between the Cultana and Moonta basement lithologies.

abstract: SALT MINING STUDY:  Field tests on the feasibility of Lake Torrens salt production to supply raw material for the planned Redcliff Petrochemical Project were continued, with project planning technical data demonstrations given to visiting officials of the Dow Chemical Co., Union Carbide Corp., B.F. Goodrich and Co., and State and Commonwealth Governments, on the progress so far achieved. Following the setting-up of a pilot plant maintenance camp and meteorological station, a series of lake brine concentrator and crystallizer ponds were constructed on Lake Torrens in April-May 1979 to trial the feasibility of producing high-quality salt there.  Subsequent salt crystallization batch testing under normal field conditions has indicated that a salt product of purity in the range 99.5-99.9% NaCl may be feasible, provided that contamination from clay and gypsum can be minimised.  Data recorded from two identical "Class A" evaporating pans, one filled with Lake Torrens brine taken from sampling trench #11, and one filled with freshwater obtained from the Yadlamalka stock watering pipeline, indicate that dense brine will evaporate onsite at a rate of 67% of that of fresh water. Pump tests of a brine pipeline test facility were also begun in November 1979, using both bare and cement-lined black steel pipes, through which brine will then be pumped for a month, after which the pipes will be cut open and examined for abrasion and for gypsum buildup.  BASE METAL EXPLORATION:  Late in 1977 a search of the licence area began, under a joint venture with Aquitaine Australia Minerals, for possible Olympic Dam - type mineralisation which might have formed in buried Middle Proterozoic bedrock lying adjacent to the Torrens Hinge Zone. Work included a detailed interpretation of existing aeromagnetic data using the Compudepth method, and also a regional gravity data interpretation; then there took place the deepening to 600.0 m, by diamond drilling, of the earlier Delhi percussion hole BDH4, plus additional deep stratigraphic rotary / diamond drilling (4 more holes totalling 2520 m), and lastly, the acquisition and interpretation of a detailed ground gravity survey near Wilga Point, and of an experimental high resolution reflection seismic survey near Beda Hill.  Only one of the latest drillholes, DDH SLT103, penetrated the pre-Adelaidean basement (non-magnetic Gawler Range Volcanics) at 614 m depth.  A locally thick and complete Adelaidean stratigraphic section, thickening to the east, is indicated by the geophysical and drilling results.  Apart from minor chalcopyrite found in the Backy Point Beds, and traces of ?bornite within the Woocalla Dolomite, no significant metallic mineralisation has yet been encountered during this search.

abstract: After a geological reconnaissance conducted in the Lake Torrens area located some surface geochemical enrichments of phosphate within an attenuated basal section of the Cambrian Andamooka Limestone at several different stratigraphic levels within that unit, it became apparent that a more complete section of this unit, including the phosphatic horizons, might exist towards the east in a more basinal setting. To test this hypothesis, a scout drilling programme of 9 vertical rotary/percussion drillholes, for a total penetration of 458 m, was completed over the inferred basin structure. The results of the drilling were not encouraging, with a highest drill sample assay value of just 0.15% P2O5 being returned, and no significantly phosphatic horizons encountered. Assays for copper, lead and zinc also failed to produce any levels of interest. The thickness of Andamooka Limestone intersected by the drillholes ranges from 22 m to 38 m, and there is a slight apparent thickening towards the centre of the basin. Typically, finely crystalline massive and occasionally vuggy dolomite overlies oolitic dolomite/limestone with intraclastic material at the base, representing marginal marine environments. No fossiliferous strata indicative of offshore deposition were seen, and the phosphatic transition horizon seen at Lake Arthur is also absent.

Data from this tenement is part of the fourth public release of historic information pertaining to a number of formerly confidential WMC Stuart Shelf licences.  WMC's first public announcement about the discovery of the giant Olympic Dam copper deposit was made at its AGM held on 18/11/1976. The orebody was found by diamond drillhole RD1 drilled on EL 190 during July 1975, with significant copper suphides (chalcocite) first recognised during a delayed inspection of that hole's retrieved drillcore during September 1975. The size of the discovery was confirmed by drillhole RD10 during early November 1976, when it encountered mineralisation grading an average 2.12% Cu over a 170 m thick cored interval within highly altered and iron-enriched pre-Adelaidean acid igneous basement rocks. After WMC had made this initial press release, the later-detected substantial uranium content of these same rocks cored by RD10 (averaging 0.58 kg/t U3O8 over 170 m) was announced in the company's next quarterly report, made public on 11/2/1977. abstract: An area located immediately west of the northern tip of Lake Torrens, and covered by the dunefield in which the head of Stuart Creek rises, was taken under licence by Western Mining Corp. (WMC) to document the stratigraphic section present on the northern margin of the Stuart Shelf. This area had not previously been explored for base metals. Specific interest centred on ascertaining whether suitable geological environments exist there for the formation of stratiform copper mineralisation in places where coincident gravity and magnetic anomalies occur. Mineralisation of the Mount Gunson, Cattle Grid deposit type, associated with the Pandurra Formation - Whyalla Sandstone unconformity, was to be sought according to one possible exploration model.  At the outset of exploration of EL 231, a large geophysical target was identified in the vicinity of Pimba Dam on Stuart Creek Station, where, on the basis of available South Australian Department of Mines' regional 4-mile geophysical coverage, a 0 mGal gravity anomaly coincides with a 6000 gamma magnetic anomaly. Following WMC's gridding and levelling of seven prospect grid lines totalling ~50 line km, detailed ground magnetic and gravity data were acquired there during May 1976 in order to be able to make estimates of the depth to top of pre-Pandurra Formation crystalline basement. Magnetic and gravity readings made at 100 m station spacings allowed such an estimate, of 600-650 m, to be made using the maximum and minimum slope characteristics of the respective data profiles. During July-November 1976, a single vertical test diamond drillhole called BD1 was completed to a total depth (TD) of 646.6 m to test the postulated basement high at the Bopeechee prospect. Basement, consisting of aplitic rock containing abundant magnetite and pyrite, was reached at a depth of 607.5 m, beneath a thick flat-lying cover sequence comprising Adelaidean Woomera (Tregolana) Shale overlain by Corraberra Sandstone and Simmens (Arcoona) Quartzite, then Cambrian Andamooka Limestone and Yarrawurta Shale. Assaying of drill core samples from the basement interval yielded 38 m @ 0.1058% Cu. The composition of the basement rock that was penetrated was thought to be suitable for sourcing the observed magnetic and gravity highs, and because of its elevated copper content, WMC expected that adjacent sedimentary basins might have some potential for carrying stratiform copper mineralisation. It was proposed that a follow-up hole should later be drilled off-structure to investigate this possibility.  A second, prominent geophysical target located near Ferguson Hill in the far north of the tenement was next chosen by WMC for delineation by detailed ground geophysical surveys, to determine if the basement there lies at an accessible depth, as preliminary aeromagnetic data interpretation had indicated that the magnetic source could lie at a depth of almost 3 km. After a break of several months, field work recommenced during April 1977, when detailed ground magnetic and gravity readings were made along a grid of seven lines put in 4 km apart at Ferguson Hill prospect, again utilising a 100 m station spacing. This work defined a moderate magnetic high of 1700 nT amplitude, partly coinciding with a broad north-west trending gravity ridge peaking at about 10 mGal. From the detailed magnetic and gravity data profiles, interpreted depths to basement of 1100 m and 1300 m respectively were generated. During August-December 1977, in an attempt to test the postulated basement high at Ferguson Hill prospect, a single vertical diamond drillhole called FHD1 was progressed to 744 m, before being stopped due to having exhausted the capacity of the drilling rig. The hole ended in shales of inferred Tapley Hill Formation, after passing through a wholly Adelaidean sedimentary sequence consisting of probable Brachina Formation and Woomera (Tregolana) Shale to 537 m, Nuccaleena Formation to 541 m, possible Whyalla Sandstone to 564.5 m, and then grey stromatolitic dolomite and grey shales to end-of-hole. Logging and sampling of this drillhole was in progress at the end of the licence period.

abstract: Exploration undertaken by Western Mining Corp. across a number of adjoining licences located to the north and north-east of Woomera, in a search for possible economic Mount Gunson - type stratiform copper mineralisation that could have formed within a sequence of buried Adelaidean metasediments of the eastern Stuart Shelf occupying the southern Arcoona Plateau region, initially comprised ground geophysical surveys aimed at delineating several interpreted regional magnetic and gravity anomalies, followed by targeted deep stratigraphic/exploratory drilling at confirmed prospects. The subject licence area lies just to the west of the north-northwest trending Torrens Hinge Zone (THZ), a major basement-penetrating structural feature which borders the Stuart Shelf and is located approximately under the western margin of Lake Torrens.  Existing deep drillhole stratigraphic information for the region was restricted to that derived from the Clarence River Basin Oil Co.'s Woomera 1 located at Phillips Pond, on the Arcoona Plateau west of the THZ, which bottomed at 611.28 m within the Late Middle Proterozoic Pandurra Formation. One favoured exploration model being addressed by WMC on the basis of the Woomera 1 stratigraphy was the possibility of copper mineralisation occurring at the Pandurra Formation - Whyalla Sandstone unconformity.  At the outset, WMC's interpretation of available 1:250,000 scale regional geophysical data, looking for associated gravity and magnetic anomalies like those observed at Mount Gunson, identified a series of six magnetic anomalies of up to 3200 gammas intensity which appeared to ring a ~20 mGal gravity anomaly centred near Arcoona Homestead. To allow estimation of the depth to basement at these magnetic features, ground magnetic and gravity survey traverses were run. Geophysical modelling of the results allowed the selection of two targets for priority drilling. While the ground geophysical surveys were in progress during mid-1976, WMC also undertook surface geochemical sampling of ironstone lag occurring in fault zones, in the hope of detecting copper which could have been scavenged from underlying horizons. All of the lag assays returned low copper values, but the ironstones outcropping at Woomera Village contained several percent of barium, an element though to be a possible pathfinder for copper.  Late in 1976, two stratigraphic/exploratory drillholes were percussion precollared into the Arcoona Quartzite. Then vertical diamond hole AD1 was drilled ahead from 136.52 m to a total depth of 510.05 m during the period December 1976-January 1977. An expected sequence of horizontally bedded metasediments of the Adelaidean Stuart Shelf section was intersected down to 485.02 m depth, and below this a fractured massive haematitic rock (? Pandurra Formation or older bedrock) was encountered. No anomalous copper values were recorded from assaying of diamond drill core samples. WMC noted a similarity in rock type between the fractured haematitic rock found at the bottom of AD1, and the rock penetrated in hole number RD7 that had recently been completed at the Olympic Dam prospect. Accordingly, it was decided to follow up this encouraging feature with further drilling in the Canegrass Swamp area. Stratigraphic diamond hole AD2 was spudded in February 1977 and was drilled vertically out of its 93.04 m deep precollar to a depth of 258 m, whereat the drilling rods became stuck. The drillhole was wedged off several times in attempts to bypass the bad ground, which caused the rods to become badly jammed again at 400 m depth. Eventually the hole was able to be progressed, and it was completed at a TD of 829 m in mid-July 1977. AD2 penetrated the basement at a depth of 812.52 m. The rocks are oxidised and strongly leached ferruginous sediments, showing bedding at about 45 degrees to the core axis. Very minor chalcopyrite occurs along partings. Several fine-grained basic igneous dykes were cored in the lowermost part of the Pandurra Formation and in this basement unit. The maximum copper value returned from the basement assays was 0.1% Cu over 2.0 m. The basement core also averaged 20 ppm U3O8, with a highest assay value of 31 ppm over 2.0 m.  Because of the elevated uranium content displayed by the bedded basement sampled in hole AD2, WMC shortly afterwards also performed uranium assays on the fractured drill core from hole AD1. These haematitic rocks are also anomalous in uranium, averaging 51 ppm U3O8 over a 24.85 m thick interval, with the lowermost 4.05 m averaging 117 ppm.  Another ground gravity and magnetic survey was conducted during June 1977 in the vicinity of Oak Dam, to further define the magnetic anomaly on which drillhole AD1 had been sited. Other ground geophysical traverses were later conducted over the Pearson Hill and Cocky Swamp magnetic features, and ongoing work was planned for the Horse Well and Winjabbie Dam features.

title: Data release [made at SA Director of Mines' discretion] : Lake Torrens (part of the Stuart Shelf Project). Progress reports to licence expiry/renewal, for the period 30/1/1976 to 29/1/1978.
notes:
Notes: This release to the public of the subject mineral exploration data, namely, company data which was acquired more than 5 years ago, is being done by DMITRE in accord with the provisions of Section 77D of the Mining Act 1971 and Regulation 88 of the Mining Regulations 2011. Data from this tenement is part of the first official such release of historic information pertaining to a number of formerly confidential WMC Stuart Shelf licences.  WMC's first public announcement about the discovery of the giant Olympic Dam copper deposit was made at its AGM held on 18/11/1976. The orebody was found by diamond drillhole RD1 drilled on EL 190 during July 1975, with significant copper suphides (chalcocite) first recognised during a delayed inspection of that hole's retrieved drillcore during September 1975. The size of the discovery was confirmed by drillhole RD10 during early November 1976, when it encountered mineralisation grading an average 2.12% Cu over a 170 m thick cored interval within highly altered and iron-enriched pre-Adelaidean acid igneous basement rocks. After WMC had made this initial press release, the later-detected substantial uranium content of these same rocks cored by RD10 (averaging 0.58 kg/t U3O8 over 170 m) was announced in the company's next quarterly report, made public on 11/2/1977.   Ministerial consent was granted on 1/3/1977 to an agreement for amalgamated licence expenditure commitments on WMC's Stuart Shelf ELs 190, 231, 232, 233, 269, 279, 292, 293 and 294.  A continuation of tenure over the same area has now been granted to WMC as EL 404.

abstract: Exploration undertaken by Western Mining Corp. in a search for possible economic Mount Gunson - type stratiform copper mineralisation that could have formed within a sequence of buried Adelaidean metasediments of the eastern Stuart Shelf which in part subcrop on EL 233, initially comprised ground geophysical surveys aimed at delineating several interpreted regional magnetic and gravity anomalies, followed by targeted deep stratigraphic/exploratory drilling at two confirmed prospects. Approximately 70% of EL 233 is covered by poorly consolidated Recent to Tertiary evaporitic and lacustrine sediments of Lake Torrens, which WMC had  estimated as being up to 300 m thick. The north-northwest trending Torrens Hinge Zone (THZ), a major basement-penetrating structural feature bordering the Stuart Shelf, was believed to underlie the western margin of the lake.  Existing deep drillhole stratigraphic information was restricted to that derived from the Clarence River Basin Oil Co.'s Woomera 1 located at Phillips Pond, on the Arcoona Plateau west of the THZ, which bottomed at 611.28 m within the Late Middle Proterozoic Pandurra Formation. One favoured exploration model being addressed by WMC on the basis of the Woomera 1 stratigraphy was the possibility of copper mineralisation occurring at the Pandurra Formation - Whyalla Sandstone unconformity.  Early in 1976, 5 traverses totalling 56 line km of ground magnetic and gravity readings taken at 100 m station intervals were laid out across semi-coincident 4000 gamma regional magnetic and 0 mGal regional gravity highs (named the Torrens prospect) mapped as extending over part of that lake adjacent to the north-eastern side of Andamooka Island, about 8 km from Crombie Ridge.  Interpretation of the resulting ground magnetic profiles TR1 and TR2 placed the top of a discrete 2000nT magnetic source body at between 500 and 550 m depth, and showed that it dips south-eastwards to 800-900 m deep over a distance of about 5 km. This model fits with the expectation that, heading eastwards across the THZ, the flat-lying shallow marine platformal sediments of the Stuart Shelf should thicken, change facies and become much more folded and faulted. Three single-point electrosoundings, performed to determine the depth to bedrock under the north-western margin of the lake, indicated that it lies at 40-50 m depth. Subsequently, a rotary airblast, cased precollar hole was drilled to 58 m depth during November 1976, after the completion of which, vertical diamond hole TD1 was drilled to a total depth of 498 m during December 1976-January 1977 from a site on the shoreline of Andamooka Island located nearest to the shallow point of the target magnetic body. Down to a depth of 412.7 m that corresponds to the base of the Tregolana Shale, this drillhole passed through relatively shallow (10-15 degrees) dipping, recognisably Adelaidean strata, but below this depth the sedimentary rocks intersected are very brecciated and have an overall steeper dip of ~30 degrees. A very brecciated and altered chemical sedimentary unit was encountered at the bottom of TD1, over the depth interval 422.75-498 m. It exhibits abundant chlorite, fluorite, pyrite and magnetite, and was found to contain up to 0.29% Cu and 27 % Fe.  To follow up another potential target on EL 233, a ground magnetic and gravity survey was conducted during January 1977 along 5 traverses located on the north-western main shoreline of the lake, close to Conan Ridge. However, apparently coinciding regional magnetic and gravity anomalies that had previously been seen at this Red Dam prospect were downgraded by WMC when the new gravity data did not record any appreciable increase in the Bouguer anomaly strength. Later in 1977, more traverses of ground geophysics were acquired in the West Well area on the north-eastern shoreline of Lake Torrens, and the results enabled that particular prospect to be confirmed for drilling. Stratigraphic/exploratory test hole WWD1 was spudded there during January 1978.

abstract: Prospecting, mapping and rock sampling were completed to assess the potential for Mount Gunson - type stratabound copper occurrences within folded Upper Proterozoic arkosic-calcareous arenites that overlie intermediate-basic volcanic rocks. Stratabound copper mineralization occurs in arkosic siltstones at Robinsons mine, where faulting and diapirism have mobilized and concentrated weak syngenetic copper mineralization. However, in the Depot Creek area generally the base metal content of both the sedimentary and volcanic rocks appears to be uniformly low.  Copper mineralization within the Depot Creek Volcanics occurs either in shear zones or quartz veins.

The use of radiometric borehole logging to identify such thin lithological units, for purposes of correlation between widely spaced holes, proved most successful in the Tregalana area.  An Honours student project was supervised which sampled volcanic rocks in drill core from diamond hole SAS1 in the northern, Tent Hill licence block, to describe and characterise the spilitic lava flows intersected there overlying the Pandurra Formation: rock textural, silicate geochemical and Rb/Sr dating geochronological evidence was presented that defines a new stratigraphic unit, the Beda Volcanics, which is well differentiated from the lithologically similar Roopena and Depot Creek alkaline basaltic volcanic rocks of the region.

abstract: 1:25,000 scale geological mapping and scout stratigraphic drilling (9 vertical rotary holes for a total penetration of 758.5 m) have outlined the general distribution of Adelaidean rocks in the Lake Macfarlane and Island Lagoon areas. Perhaps the most important feature, from an exploration point of view, is the local geometry of the post-Pandurra Formation erosion surface which controls the distribution of later sediments and is host to known copper mineralisation near Mount Gunson. This surface is exposed on the western edge of Lake Macfarlane, and slopes away to the east to form a broad shallow basin.  Interpretation of geophysical data has shown a number of major faults, fractures and basic igneous dykes in the Carpentarian basement. Whilst on a broad scale such features may have affected the distribution of stratabound base metal deposition, the individual faults, fractures and dykes are not considered to be exploration targets.  The apparent stratigraphic prerequisites for forming Mount Gunson type mineralisation (i.e. Whyalla Sandstone overlying Pandurra Formation) are not present in the Island Lagoon area. There are indications of base metal mineralisation present in shaly facies of the Tapley Hill Formation, but exploration to date has not indicated any specific target zones.

abstract: Possible buried stratabound copper mineralisation of Mount Gunson / Cattlegrid type was the target of exploration performed on an area of the Stuart Shelf located 60 km east of Woomera.  After conducting detailed 1:12,000 and 1:16,000 scale geological mapping which disclosed two places where surface copper mineralisation could be seen associated with the Corraberra Sandstone Member, a programme of stratigraphic/exploratory percussion and diamond drilling was undertaken targeting subtle magnetic anomalies.  No significant mineralisation was disclosed by this drilling (11 vertical percussion holes totalling 1852 m, and 3 diamond holes aggregating 1033.75 m below the percussion precollars), but valuable stratigraphic insights were gained. The target basal Adelaidean sequence overlies the top of Pandurra Formation unconformity surface, which does not outcrop within the licence, but appears to lie at over 200 m below the ground surface across most of the tenement.  However, both new field mapping and drill core evidence, wherein large pebbles of Gawler Range Volcanics and even larger boulders of granite, that are obviously derived from the basement, were seen in conglomerates of the Tent Hill Formation and older Adelaidean units, imply that a basement high must be present in the subsurface somewhere locally, and should be actively sought.  A new aeolian sandstone unit, lying unconformably between the Pandurra Formation and the Tapley Hill Formation, has lately been recognised from studies of drill cores recovered from diamond holes SASC1 and SASC2, and holes SAR3 and SAR4 from the neighbouring EL 389 to the south.  This unit was also intersected in percussion hole PSC6.  Informally named the "Yeltacowie Sandstone", it appears to occupy the same stratigraphic position as the Backy Point Beds known from further south on the Stuart Shelf.  However, it has not been seen to exist in the area west of EL 261, and may pinch out there against topographically higher Pandurra Formation.  The presence of weakly anomalous base metal geochemical values in hole SASC2 (ranging up to 710 ppm Cu, 140 ppm Zn and 16 ppm U across the basal 18 m of Pandurra Formation and upper 5 m of weakly foliated biotitic granite basement) prompted petrographic and petrophysical examinations of these rocks to find out the nature of the basement, and to ascertain whether the very fine-grained sulphide minerals in the matrix of the Pandurra Formation conglomerate could possibly be detected under the deep cover by gravity survey methods.  Petrology showed that the gneissic basement has been extensively deformed and altered, with pervasive haematite - specularite - sericite - chlorite, and thus has similarities to the granite at Mount Woods.  Specific gravity measurements taken on 214 drill core sections were analysed statistically, and the corresponding density differences were calculated for the thickness of mineralised conglomerate and that of the rocks known to lie above it.  Based on this information, the anomalous gravity effect of a thin tabular source lying within the Pandurra Formation conglomerate was calculated as 0.07 mGal, which is too small a response to register as an anomaly on a gravity survey.

abstract: During renewed tenure, under two sequential licences, of an area located 60 km east of Woomera, exploration has continued to seek possible buried economic copper mineralisation of Mount Gunson or, preferably, Olympic Dam type.  New work has included the acquisition and interpretation of an detailed airborne magnetic - radiometric survey (Austirex, 1980 : 412 line km on 30 east-west lines spaced 300 m apart, at 120 m flight height), plus ground magnetic and gravity surveying, and percussion (2 holes, total 952 m) and diamond drilling (1 hole, 1250 m cored). The airborne survey has confirmed, located and more accurately defined the broad, 120 nT magnetic high and associated low evident to the south-west of Archie Beavis Dam.  The anomaly does not appear to have a point-pole geometry, but is an assymetric feature interpreted to be due to an east-northeast trending elongate body.  Reconnaissance gravity traverses over this magnetic anomaly (73 stations 500 m apart along 5 traverses totalling 33 line km) show a broad weak gravity high centred somewhat north-west of the supposed magnetic source. Multi-element geochemical analyses were done on samples of sawn drill core from the target basal Pandurra Formation and the underlying basement in Seltrust's previously drilled DDH SASC2 and DDH SASC3.  In the basal haematitic conglomerate section of SASC2 (depth interval 509.7-516.7 m) there is weakly anomalous Cu (500 ppm) plus anomalous Mn (2000 ppm), Fe2O3 (17-34%) and La (166-368 ppm).  No significant results were returned from SASC3, which lacks the pebble conglomerate within its basal Pandurra Formation interval. New percussion drillhole PSC12 was put down to 352 m depth in February-March 1981 as a precollar to test the Archie Beavis magnetic anomaly, but was not continued with diamond coring because the drill location was subsequently deemed unsuitable for properly testing this anomaly, which has an interpreted source depth 650 m below ground level, and modelled body dimensions of 2450 m x 2750 m. A reconnaissance ground gravity survey was run over the entire licence area during July-September 1982, on east-west lines 1 km apart, with stations at 500 m intervals.  The aim was to locate dense bodies not necessarily associated with magnetic anomalies.  The survey revealed a small gravity anomaly in the order of 1 mGal just to the south of the drillhole SASC2 location, which was later confirmed by more detailed gravity coverage.  This "Bowman gravity anomaly" was tested by a 600 m deep percussion drillhole (PSC13) in June 1983, which penetrated haematised crystalline basement at 518 m depth beneath a 10 m thickness of derived conglomerate.  Diamond drillhole SASC4 was wedged-off from PSC13 at 472 m to test the lithologies at the metasedimentary sequence contact with the basement, and to take core of the basement.  This hole had reached 521 m depth at the end of the current reporting period (date of Salt Creek licence renewal as EL 1170), still drilling within haematitic, feldspar porphyry conglomerate: the hole was later continued to a total depth of 1250 m, remaining in the same brecciated material throughout.

abstract: Brownfields copper exploration undertaken by WMC in the Phillips Ridge area, located about 24 km east-southeast of the Olympic Dam discovery, initially consisted of the acquisition of gravity and ground magnetic traverses across a regional gravity anomaly which it was hoped might be a continuation of the Olympic Dam coincident magnetic and gravity geophysical feature. However, the newly detailed gravity anomaly at Phillips Ridge showed less symmetry, and appeared to be a more complicated feature. Three possible drilling sites were chosen nevertheless, and in May 1977 a single vertical diamond drillhole, PD1a, was completed to a total depth of 414 m at one of them, bottoming beneath a fault zone in a leucocratic, banded biotite-rich gneiss. This drillhole encountered a green, chloritic quartz-veined basaltic rock at 336 m depth, which contained minor pyrite and chalcopyrite (best drill core assay result 7.5 m @ 0.25% Cu from 340 m depth). The metavolcanic unit, which is 18 m thick, overlies chlorite, haematite and sericite - altered granitic basement. While the results of this drilling were being evaluated, attention was shifted to another regional gravity anomaly present in the vicinity of Bills Lookout, immediately east of the Andamooka Opalfield. After some delays experienced in gaining on-ground access, further gravity (1624 stations read) and ground magnetic surveying was performed in this location. A strong positive gravity anomaly was detected that coincides with a strong negative magnetic anomaly, approximately 2 km north-east of Teatree Dam. abstract: Stratigraphic diamond drillhole BLD1, drilled vertically by Western Mining Corp. during the period April-May 1979 out of a 160 m deep percussion precollared hole to test a coincident gravity and magnetic anomaly located north-east of Teatree Dam, was completed at a total depth of 768 m in altered gabbroic intrusive rocks, which explained the targeted negative magnetic anomaly.
