abstract: A prominent regional aeromagnetic anomaly of unknown source depth, that is situated north-west of Roxby Downs along the strike of the Torrens Hinge Zone structural lineament, and which lies close to an intersection of other major lineaments, has been explored for possible Olympic Dam type basement-hosted base metal and precious metal mineralisation. Based on ground gravity and magnetic data newly acquired at this Trecompana Hill anomaly, a likely future exploratory drilling target was identified, pending a review to be made after the completion by the Newmont joint venture of a separate deep diamond drillhole and associated seismic reflection survey at the Joe's Dam magnetic anomaly lying on an adjacent licence along strike to the south. However, the results of the work carried out on EL 335 showed that there the Adelaidean cover metasediments are more than 1500 m thick, and so the depth to the top of the pre-Adelaidean basement could not be established. In view of this setback, Newmont concluded that a similar thickness of cover would exist on the subject EL 440, meaning that drill testing of the Trecompana Hill anomaly could not be economically justified.

notes:

abstract: As part of earning a 40% JV interest in the NBH Port Pirie licence area, Aquitaine (Australia) Minerals Pty Ltd has been using gravity and magnetics to try to define new drilling targets.  During the period July to September 1980, microbarometer-levelled gravity stations were read at 500 m intervals on five traverses in the northern part of the main Wandearah anomaly trend, near the Broughton River.  This data has been interpreted and a vertical diamond drillhole to at least 600 m depth is planned. The main conclusions drawn from the latest geophysical review were: - 1. A large, dense magnetic body is present in the basement; it trends NNW-SSE. 2. This body has been intruded near its southern end by highly magnetic rocks. 3. There is a basement high which generally follows the magnetic-gravity trend.  Some of the highs are oblique to this trend and appear to be tectonically controlled. The gravity data were separated into regional and residual anomalies.  Exploratory DDH PP19 is situated on one of these residual anomalies, considered to be due to either a basement horst or haematitic sediments within the basement.

abstract: Exploration for possible economic basement-hosted Roxby Downs style base metal sulphide deposits was undertaken in an area located approximately 90 km north-west of Woomera. Existing regional geophysical airborne survey coverage was too sparse to adequately define drill targets, so a more detailed low-level aeromagnetic and aerial radiometric survey (of 1750 line km at 800 m flight line spacing and 90 m sensor elevation) was carried out to try to map discrete anomalies for subsequent ground geophysical delineation. Problems of poor quality management in data acquisition and processing by the contractor led to delays in follow-up work, and uncertainty about selecting which were the best anomalies to ground truth. Ultimately only a small number of low priority magnetic/gravity anomalies were defined, of which two were selected for drill testing. Two vertical rotary percussion drillholes were completed in early 1979, both penetrating to the rig's nominal depth capability of 400 m. Each hole bottomed when still within the inferred upper to middle part of the Pandurra Formation, and therefore the targeted top of the crystalline basement was expected to lie several hundred metres below. Consequently the source of the drilled geophysical anomalies could not be explained. No base metal values of significance were found in downhole geochemical sampling, and no subsurface radiation peaks  were detected.

abstract: The subject quarterly reports record primarily the progress and results of surface and underground exploratory drilling designed to define the Olympic Dam orebody. Further brief comments are provided about the establishment of mining and mineral processing infrastructure, and updated locational plans are included for the activities/features mentioned.  During the period of maximum appraisal activity, from early 1981 until mid-1984, up to 13 surface diamond drilling rigs and five underground diamond drilling rigs, working 2 shifts/day, were in use. Geological logs for the resulting drillholes are reported herein, and significant mineralised intercepts that were found are summarised.  The Whenan Shaft, sunk at the position of surface drillhole RD100, was excavated to a total depth of 500 m over the period December 1980 - August 1982. After its completion, a campaign of underground exploratory drilling began in May-June 1982 from platforms established at the -420 m level in the shaft. When a sufficient amount of drillhole information about the orebody had been collected by this means, underground drive development was begun in early 1984, initially starting from the -320 m and -380 m levels in Whenan Shaft, and proceeding southwards from the shaft into a part of the deposit where high gold values had been indicated in raw assay results of diamond drill cores recovered by surface drilling. At the same time, following on from a site preparation and build phase that commenced in July 1983, a newly commissioned 5 tonnes/hour metallurgical processing pilot plant was used to test treat bulk parcels of copper-uranium ore extracted from the underground development openings. The pilot plant ran initially for ten months, from February to November 1984, producing 509 dry tonnes of copper concentrates from the grinding and flotation circuit, which were shipped to Finland to undergo smelting trials. In August 1984, an on-site Sirosmelt furnace was also commissioned to produce trial products of matte and blister copper.  From early 1985 onwards, underground development driving at Olympic Dam was focussed on providing access to rich copper-uranium ore zones that had been defined at some distance to the north-west of Whenan Shaft, as well as continuing to drive acess tunnels into the southern gold zone. From the middle of 1985 onwards, copper concentrates produced by the restarted pilot plant were upgraded in a newly completed uranium leaching and reflotation circuit, to investigate optimum ways of reducing the uranium content in the feed concentrates that would be destined for smelting, and thus allow the WMC to produce a commercially acceptable copper metal output. At this time, the primary flotation circuit tailings were still not being processed to extract any uranium.  During March 1986, excavation commenced of a transport portal for a service decline (road) from the surface, starting from a site located immediately to the north-west of Whenan Shaft. The decline was intended to connect the now extensive underground workings (with the shallowest being at the -260 m level) with the existing surface installations. At about this time, construction of surface facilities for the WMC's planned first stage full-scale mining and ore treatment operation was also commenced.

abstract: Ongoing exploration by WMC of an area located in the Andamooka district, which surrounds  the township and opalfield region at some little distance, and which, some 25 km to the west of the town includes the Roxby Downs prospect on which the giant Olympic Dam copper-uranium-gold deposit discovery was made in July 1975, has consisted of the further appraisal of selected geophysical anomalies by ground-based gravity and magnetic traversing, leading to deep exploratory percussion/diamond core drilling.    Near the start of its term, part of the licence area was overflown by the detailed airborne magnetic/radiometric survey conducted for WMC and BP during the period September-November 1979 (total coverage 32,441 line km flown along 400 m spaced north-south lines with a 100 m sensor height above ground surface). Ground magnetic and gravity surveys were completed at the Wirrda Well prospect, located 5 km north-east of Coorlay Dam and about 28 km south-southeast of Olympic Dam. They defined near-coincident gravity and magnetic anomalies, with an estimated depth to magnetic source body of 500 m. It was decided to diamond drill this prospect later in the year, and so a 230 m deep precollar hole was percussion drilled there.  Following the drilling in mid-1979 of a vertical RAB precollar to 111.75 m depth at the Acropolis prospect, located 11 km west-southwest of Appendicitis Dam and ~24 km south-west of the Olympic Dam deposit, exploratory/stratigraphic diamond drillhole ACD1 was completed there at a total depth of 1097.6 m, on 24/1/1980. Pre-Pandurra Formation basement was reached at a depth of 717.8 m, and was found to be anomalous in both copper and uranium throughout the interval drilled, where the rocks consisted of haematite-rich slightly mineralised volcanic sediments overlying sericitized, brecciated porphyrytic felsic volcanic flows having abundant magnetitic veining and trace to minor bornite in addition to disseminated chalcopyrite and pyrite. The most significant drill core sample assay results were 8 m @ 0.09% Cu and 464 ppm U3O8 from the depth interval 818-826 m within the volcanic sediments, and 66 m @ 0.7% Cu and 35 ppm U3O8 from the depth interval 924-990 m at the top of the underlying porphyritic volcanic zone. The drillhole was later wireline geophysically logged down to 944 m depth, but the tool could not pass any deeper due to hole collapse. Detailed grid-based gravity surveying of the Acropolis prospect was completed in May 1980, and the results showed that the centre of the gravity anomaly is approximately 1 km east of the anomaly centre defined by the 1977 survey, chosen as the site of the ACD1 test drillhole.  Ground gravity and magnetic surveys were completed at the Bills Lookout/Bills Lookout North and Saddle Hill prospects in July 1980, and a decision was made to test the eastern gravity high of the Bills Lookout anomaly complex.  Exploratory/stratigraphic drilling of the large Wirrda Well prospect commenced in March 1980. Diamond drillhole WRD1 was completed at TD 982.2 m on 29/7/1980. Below 355.45 m depth it penetrated a basement succession consisting of altered volcanic rocks, polymict sedimentary breccia, altered granites and altered felsic intrusive rocks. Bornite and chalcopyrite were recorded as occurring sporadically in haematite veins encountered below 592 m depth (best result 1.37% Cu over the depth interval 695-700 m). The haematite veins also display weakly anomalous radioactivity (best assay result 71 ppm U3O8 over the depth interval 832-958 m). When an attempt was made during the third quarter of 1980 to run wireline geophysical logs in this drillhole, it was unsuccessful due to hole blockage. Diamond drillhole WRD2, percussion precollared to 300 m depth at a location ~1.8 km south-southwest of WRD 1, was completed at TD 934.5 m on 8/12/1980. Below 452 m depth this hole encountered a thick interval of Olympic Dam type granite breccia containing minor chalcopyrite mineralisation (to 0.34% Cu). In addition, 1.0% Co was recorded over the depth interval 912-915 m. Following the acquisition of detailed gravity readings over the Wirrda Well East gravity high, a third diamond hole, WRD3, was completed there late in 1980. Preliminary information given herein states that no mineralisation is present in this hole.

abstract: Ongoing copper exploration in the Mount Gunson area was directed primarily at locating economic stratiform mineralisation in the Tapley Hill Formation, which overlies Pandurra Formation and the associated Cattlegrid orebody.  New work comprised acquisition of CSAMT, gravity and ground magnetic surveys, RC drilling (877 holes, total 10,154 m), diamond drilling (49 holes, total 1834 m), and further metallurgical investigations of mineralised material from several previously identified prospects. An indicated resource of 1 Mt @ 1.5% Cu was outlined at the MG14 deposit.  Flotation testing done on milled samples of ore from this orebody showed that a 15% Cu concentrate product could be achieved at >75% recovery from a 1.5% head grade, provided that the process water quality was maintained at <19000 ppm TDS. Groundwater and vegetation surveys were performed by contractors to guide the licensees' evaluation of the water supply, tailings disposal and environmental impact minimisation requirements of likely mining operations.  Anomalous lead and zinc were intersected in the north-eastern part of the licence area around Elizabeth Creek (best assay values being 1.4% Zn and 0.21% Pb over a 2 m interval from 304 m depth). Basement drilling, to follow up both gravity / magnetic targets and Cu anomalies from earlier holes, intersected un-mineralised granite and Hutchison Group.

abstract: In the latter stages of its search for possible economic base and precious metal deposits in the Bute area, North Broken Hill targeted the concealed pre-Adelaidean basement rocks for Mount Gunson or ?Olympic Dam type hydrothermal ores, and for Mount Isa type sedex ores, by continuing with exploratory diamond drilling based on auger geochemical bedrock sampling and the results of reconnaissance and detailed ground magnetic, gravity and induced polarisation surveys. The percussion precollared diamond drilling (28 holes totalling 4855.48 m) was useful in uncovering a great deal of new local stratigraphic information and in pointing to the causes of observed geophysical anomalies, but it did not reveal any metal mineralisation of note.  It appears that near Bute there are an abundance of basic intrusive rocks within the Carpentarian basement, when compared to the Moonta region, besides the expected granitic porphyry and gneissic rocks, amphibolites and strongly hydrothermally altered dolomites and other chemical sedimentary lithologies.  Due to the stratigraphic and tectonic complexity of this area of the Torrens Hinge Zone, even after 6 year's work NBH is not sure of its true mineral potential, other than to conclude that, despite the common presence of dispersed trace copper sulphides (< 0.15% Cu) near the Carpentarian - Adelaidean unconformity, a substantial near-surface metallic mineral occurrence is unlikely.

abstract: The principal target of ongoing exploration in the southern Lake Torrens region was a possible buried, large, high-grade base and precious metal deposit lying within the pre- Pandurra Formation basement.  After completing the drilling of DDH YAD1 at Yadlamalka early in 1982, and also acquiring a small ground gravity survey there, a synthesis and review of all Stuart Shelf data was carried out.  A lithogeochemical study of acid volcanic rocks encountered at the bottom of several recent deep drillholes showed that all of them could be correlated with a part of the basement volcanic section intersected at Mount Gunson.  The barium concentration was elevated in several holes, but anomalous mineralisation was not detected.  A thermoluminescence study of quartz grains in the Pandurra Fm was undertaken. The linear magnetic anomaly at Yadlamalka was interpreted as being due to a shallow, dyke - like body intruding the Adelaidean strata.  After conducting some ground magnetic surveys, stratigraphic hole YAD2 was drilled to test this interpretation.  It intersected flat lying or shallowly east dipping Beda Volcanics at a depth of 192 m.  Elevated base metal values were present at the unconformable breccia - regolith contact between the Beda Volcanics and overlying lower Burra Group siltstones, but were not considered worthy of further investigation.

abstract: An area 100 km north of Kingoonya which exhibits a strong regional gravity high and other, intersecting pronounced crustal geophysical features was acquired to search for an Olympic Dam type of base/precious metals deposit.  Semi-detailed and detailed ground magnetic and gravity surveys were performed to delineate targets, which were subsequently drilled with 10 percussion holes totalling 570 m, and sampled for geochemical and petrological analyses.  The drilled near-coincident gravity and magnetic anomalies were adequately explained, and are of no direct economic importance.  Briefly, the drilling revealed that Lower Proterozoic haematitic banded iron formations, schists and gneisses form a shallowly subcropping local palaeo-high beneath Cainozoic cover, which is bounded on both the north and south, possibly by faulting, by Carpentarian age greenschist facies metasediments and basic metavolcanics.  The BIFs contain up to 760 ppm Zn and the basement schists up to 480 ppm Cu.  The Carpentarian metasediments are locally pyritic and chloritic, and contain up to 160 ppm Pb and 430 ppm Zn.

abstract: Following a review of existing regional geophysical and geological data for the north-western Stuart Shelf, grid-based gravity and ground magnetic surveys were run to further outline two broad gravity highs associated with discrete magnetic anomalies, which it was hoped might have potential for Olympic Dam style Cu-U-Au deposits.  These features were tested by 2 diamond drillholes.  DP2 entered un-mineralised Pandurra Formation below the Mesozoic cover, and remained in it over the depth interval 204.5 - 860 m.  DP1 (total depth 616.6 m) entered volcanics of a similar density to the Pandurra Formation at 166 m depth.  Geochemical and petrographic analyses of the DP1 volcanics, which included both acid and basic material, indicated affinities with both the Gawler Range and Roopena Volcanics, but no genetic relationship to the younger Beda Volcanics. A subsequent detailed gravity survey indicated the existence of a fault between the two drill sites, which probably accounts for the major stratigraphic displacement between them.  Water sampling of 13 bores in the vicinity showed no significant uranium values. As part of a second-stage joint venture exploration programme, minor quantities of kimberlite indicator minerals were recovered from the No. 10 Creek and Paisley Creek areas, but are thought to be related to secondary sources.  Extensive follow-up stream sampling, bulk sediment sampling, ground magnetic surveys, trenching of shallow anomalies, and remote sensing investigations of geological structures, all yielded negative results for disclosing microdiamonds or kimberlite targets.

name: mesac9090
title: Francis Swamp (part of the Stuart Range Joint Venture Project). Progress report to to the end of the Newmont JV agreement exploration phase, for the period 21/8/1979 to 9/5/1980.
notes:

abstract: As part of an ongoing multi-licence programme of exploration for Roxby Downs / Olympic Dam style copper-gold-uranium [IOCG-U] mineralisation that might exist along the eastern margin of the Stuart Shelf, the licensees took up the Francis Swamp area in August 1979.  Initial work comprised making a review of available drillhole information and preparing to conduct surface-based geophysical and geochemical surveys. A stratigraphic analysis performed for EL 521 suggested that here the thickness of Adelaidean and Palaeozoic cover on basement would probably be less than it is on the JV's adjoining EL 335 to the south-east. Exploratory drilling is therefore planned for EL 521 to test the basement prospectivity beneath the south-eastern end of the Boorthanna Trough.  A programme of geochemical sampling of artesian groundwater being actively discharged through surface mound springs was undertaken during the report period. The exploration premise was that since these springs lie along prominent lineaments probably denoting fault zones, where these faults penetrate to basement the circulating groundwater rising from there may contain dissolved elements reflecting the basement geochemistry. Samples were collected of recent precipitates from the springs' outflow, and assayed for a limited number of pathfinder elements. No significant results were returned.

abstract: When Getty Oil took over management of the Stuart Range Project licences, it reviewed all of Newmont's drillhole data and undertook reclogging of the drill cores with the aim of correlating stratigraphy across the project area.  Starting in October 1980, a contract programme of geochemical sampling of groundwater and mound spring deposits was conducted by Australian Groundwater Consultants, and further grid-based ground geophysical surveys were commissioned for ELs 556, 623 and 624, where two additional regional gravity/magnetic anomalies had been recognised and required confirmation.  By end December 1980, the new JV partners had finished their stratigraphic compilation of all drillhole data from the project area. The results suggested that Carpentarian basement rocks, which are believed to host the Olympic Dam mineralisation, as not yet encountered and thus probably lying below hole TDs throughout the JV area, are too deep to warrant further exploration for targets of this type. The geochemical sampling results were also received and assessed. The assay values returned for uranium are too low to justify any ongoing exploration for secondary uranium mineralisation within the Permian and younger cover sediments. Detailed reconnaissance ground magnetic and gravity surveys acquired during October-November 1980 at the two regional geophysical features, with 600 and 590 station readings taken at 100 m intervals along lines spaced 2 km and 1 km apart respectively, failed to reveal any anomalies worthy of drilling.  The final report submitted in March 1981 included all outstanding geochemical, geophysical, petrological and oil shale analysis data not provided in the earlier joint reports.

notes:

Geographic Locality: Stuart Creek Station;1980 Trecompana Gravity Survey;1980 Chamber Creek Gravity Survey

abstract: Data from detailed gravity and ground magnetic surveys acquired over the Chambers Creek and Trecompana exploration reconnaissance grids has been interpreted to deduce whether, due to local uplift, possibly prospective basement occurs there within 500 to 800 m depth below the surface. With time spent exploring in the region, it had progressively become apparent to Getty that moving southwards over the northern Stuart Shelf there is a marked uplift in the top of basement unconformity between Newmont's drillhole SR17/2 and Olympic Dam, from >1500 m depth to 300-350 m depth. A structural model was therefore constructed, using additional drillhole data from recent intervening holes that were obtained from Amoco Minerals and Western Mining Corp., plus observed steep gradients in areromagnetic data, which proposed the existence of a NE-SW orientated step-faulted area running about 23 km north-west of Olympic Dam, across which the basement becomes downthrown by ~500 m. The subject geophysical data was acquired across the south-eastern side of the project acreage, as near to this feature as possible, to better define the probable basement depths and structures.  Interpretation of the new detailed gravity and magnetic data failed to locate geophysical anomalies of Olympic Dam type that are sourced within 800 m of the ground surface. In view of this finding, it was recommended that no further exploration work be done on the Stuart Range JV Project licences.

In later work, five aeromagnetic anomalies were drilled to test for kimberlite targets, via 10 shallow PU series rotary holes totalling 171 m.  No magnetic source was located for three of the anomalies, but the other two were shown to be caused by maghemite and magnetic sandstone occurrences present within the first few metres of the subsurface.

abstract: In a trial Mini-Sosie reflection seismic survey carried out over a 750 m section of exploration grid line near Myall Creek, where the method consisted of 6-fold profiling at 5 m trace spacing, the unconformity at the base of the Tapley Hill Formation was clearly mapped, and a potential structural low in it detected. A trial Maxiprobe survey (a vertical EM electrical sounding method) was run to try to pick faults that might define the edges of Beda Volcanics lava flows, but the method used here requires further experimentation.  A 5 km long Mini Sosie seismic reflection survey spread centred on hole CU9 indicated that the subsurface topography of the pre - Tapley Hill unconformity plane is not flat-lying as was assumed, but is markedly undulose and varied. name: mesac24882
title: Data release [made at SA Director of Mines' discretion] : Stuart Shelf and Andamooka Opalfields (the Stuart Shelf Joint Venture Project) . Progress reports to licences' expiry/renewal, for the period 16/1/1981 to 16/6/1986. [ Index Part 3 of 3 ].
notes:
Geographic Locality: Olympic Dam;1985 Snake Gully East Gravity Survey
Doc No: Env 03927
Drillhole: OFD3;(277502);HRD2;(277538);BLD4;(277528);TOD3;(277569);AD8;(20724);RED2;(20772)
Drillhole Unit No: 6336 00065;6237 00443;6337 00060;6237 00444;6335 00113;6336 00044
abstract: (Abstract continued):  During the first quarter of 1985, diamond drillhole OFD3 was completed at TD 498 m at a site 2 km west of hole OFD2, to further investigate the magnetic high south of the Opal Field. This hole reached basement at 359 m depth, passing into a 24 m thick fine grained altered felsic porphyry which is intruded by numerous dykes and veins of microgranite. The unit is sericitised and chloritised, is veined and mottled by haematite, and also has minor secondary K-feldspar and some barite. This lithology, which WMC regarded as possibly either extrusive or intrusive, was not intersected in OFD2; however, the underlying fresh granite is very similar to that seen in OFD2, as it is also cut by dykes of aplitic microgranite. Diamond drillhole HRD2 at Horn Ridge was completed at TD 454 m, after reaching basement at 327 m which consists of fresh coarse-grained hornblende(+ biotite) adamellite with minor disseminated pyrite. A small ground magnetic and gravity survey was conducted at Snake Gully East during April 1985. From the processed survey results, it was evident that there is no significant gravity anomaly associated with the Snake Gully East magnetic high.  During the second quarter of 1985, diamond drillhole BLD4 was put down at Bills Lookout, but owing to exhausting the capacity of the drilling rig, had to be terminated at 1035 m without reaching pre-Adelaidean basement. The basement depth at this site had been predicted to be around 900 m, but in light of actuality, it was clear that the Torrens Hinge Zone must take a very steep dive under this northern side of the prospect (modelling of the Bills Lookout magnetic anomaly had indicated a likely depth to magnetic source of ~1600 m, but such source was interpreted to an intra-basement body, as is the main magnetic source at Olympic Dam). No significant assay values were returned fron analyses of BLD4 drill core samples. The Adelaidean sequence seen in the BLD4 drill core has several unusual aspects. Between the Tregolana Shale and Tapley Hill Formation are two distinct (but thin) units - a diamictite and a cross-bedded arenite, possibly equivalent to Reynella Siltstone and Willochra Subgroup respectively. The Tapley Hill Formation includes several stromatolitic horizons. Beneath the Tapley Hill Formation is an 11 m thick section of coarse cobble-bearing diamictite of probable glacial origin. This unit has been tentatively correlated with the Sturtian tillites of the Adelaide area. The tillites overlie an interval containing micaceous quartzites, magnesite beds and carbonate conglomerates which are believed to represent the upper part of the Burra Group. If this correlation is correct, it denotes the first occurrence of Burra Group sediments on the Stuart Shelf.   During the third quarter of 1985, diamond drillhole TOD3 at Todds Dam was completed at TD 850 m, after reaching basement at 695 m depth, which consists of partly garnetiferous quartz-biotite schists and thin intercalated mafic units. The well-developed foliation is very steep, usually sub-parallel to the drill core axis. Local patchy sulphide accumulations are present, mainly pyrite with minor chalcopyrite, and one fist-sized chunk of arsenopyrite was noted. The best core sample assay result was 2.3 m @ 1.25% Cu, 0.27% Zn and 25 ppm Ag, while several more 2 m wide intervals grading >0.5% Cu are present in this hole: however, other trace elements returned uniformly low values. The top of basement in TOD3 is slightly deeper than in TOD2, located 2 km away to the NNW. The overlying cover sequence includes Tapley Hill Formation and Pandurra Formation, neither of which are present in TOD2. Drillhole AD8 at Arcoona South, located approximately 800 m south-west of hole AD2 at Oak Dam West, was completed to TD 1000.2 m to test part of the Canegrass gravity high. Basement was reached at 627 m depth, and consists of chlorite-haematite BIF in the upper portion (magnetitic below 858 m depth), overlying well-sorted, unaltered arkosic sediments. Downhole geophysical logs, including temperature recording, were run in both of the latest completed holes.  During the fourth quarter of 1985, diamond drillhole RED2, located at the edge of Lake Torrens near Red Dam on Andamooka Station, was completed to TD 687 m. Pre-Adelaidean basement was reached at 311 m depth, and consists of variably altered felsic volcanic or high level intrusive rocks with chloritised phenocrysts, that are sometimes veined by haematite and minor sulphides. At greater depth this lithology passes into an even-grained granitoid that resembles the rock drilled in holes OFD2 and OFD3.  On 17/12/1985, short-lived 'holding' ELs 1316 and 1317 were issued to WMC at renewal of term for its Stuart Shelf licences, to replace former ELs 784 and 993 respectively. The new licences carried no specific expenditure commitment, and therefore WMC chose to temporarily cease field work and drilling activities, instead focussing on compiling its accumulated exploration data, including completing a backlog of drill core geological logging, and then making technical presentations to potential joint venture partners. Another important task undertaken by WMC in the ensuing 6-month period was the preparation of a partial relinquishment report for the reduction in the company's Stuart Shelf acreage that was incumbent upon it under the terms of the Olympic Dam and Stuart Shelf Indenture Agreement that it had made with the South Australian Government. This condition required that WMC's 14,675 square km area of EL tenure be reduced to 3000 square km, no later than 30/6/1986. The finished relinquishment report was submitted to the South Australian Department of Mines and Energy on 20/6/1986 (see Env 6562). Following a careful review of its contents, a request for missing data identified in various categories was sent to WMC in late July 1986, and much additional data and vital record information was consequently supplied to SADME in early September. This less formally presented data and advice has now been attached to the end of the subject Envelope.

During the 32 month currency of the joint venture, BP's investment entity Roxby Management Services spent almost $10.5 million in dollars-of-the-day underwriting WMC's exploration works.
Geographic Locality: Andamooka Island;Arcoona Plateau;Lake Torrens;Murdie Island;1984 Acropolis East Gravity Survey
Doc No: Env 03927
Drillhole: WRD12;(277583);ACD8;(277522);AD5;(349230);AD5 W1;(349231);WRD13;(277584);AD6;(277551);ACD10;(18172);ASD2;(20723);WRD14;(277585);WRD15;(277586);WRD16;(262011);ACD12;(262099);AD7;(277552);OFD2;(277554)
Drillhole Unit No: 6236 00079;6335 00112;6236 00127
abstract: (Abstract continued):  During the first quarter of 1983, WMC continued acquiring complex resistivity (CR) survey data on EL 784 as the prime tool for selecting new intra-prospect drilling targets. Additional ground CR traverses were read at Wirrda Well, and initial CR coverages were obtained at Burden Hill and Todds Dam. As an aid to interpretation of the CR data, downhole electrical logs were run in more of the recently completed drillholes on the surveyed prospects; six open holes were logged at Acropolis, Wirrda Well and Olympic Dam. The newly completed regional gravity survey of the area west of Lake Torrens defined two elongate gravity highs not previously known, which are located near Cowan Ridge and Edge Hill respectively. New drillholes completed for the quarter were WRD12, ACD8 and AD5. Hole ACD8, located on the northern side of the Acropolis South-east magnetic anomaly, reached basement at 790 m depth, 150 m deeper than in ACD3 located 1 km to the south. This finding confirmed the major variation in thickness of the Pandurra Formation in the Acropolis area, as overlying units within the cover sequence are of relatively uniform thickness. The basement consists of massive to sheared, haematite and sericite-altered megacrystic granite, which is unmineralised down to the drillhole's TD of 910 m.  During the second quarter of 1983, diamond drillholes were completed at Wirrda Well (WRD13) and Oak Dam (AD6). Several intervals with anomalously high radioactivity were logged in the latter drillhole, within haematite-rich brecciated granitic rocks similar to those encountered in hole AD1. Wireline geophysical logging of previously completed drillholes was continued, with 13 holes logged.  During the third quarter of 1983, CR surveys were conducted at Cowan Ridge and Bills Lookout West, but the results were disappointing, with weak resistivity responses amongst noisy data, that could not be substantiated by phase decoupling. The intense magnetic low evident at Bills Lookout thus remained unexplained. Diamond drillhole ACD10 was completed to TD 807.5 m at Acropolis, after reaching basement at 550.5 m. Only very minor copper mineralisation and weak radioactivity was recorded (highest assay results being 0.47% Cu, 0.09 ppm U3O8, 0.03 ppm Au, 9.57 ppm Ag, 1000 ppm La and 1800 ppm Ce from certain thin intervals between 670.5 and TD).  During the fourth quarter of 1983, a CR survey was conducted at Snake Gully East, which identified a resistivity low and coincident 3-point phase anomaly 200 m east of previously completed drillhole SGD5. The conductive zone cored in SGD5 consists of pebble conglomerate and breccia with black haematite clasts and matrix, lying at the palaeosurface of weakly altered microsyenite, over the depth interval 446-457 m. This section of the drillhole included an intercept of 1.3 m @ 2.3% Cu.  Another 12 holes were logged geophysically.  During the first quarter of 1984, ground magnetic and gravity surveys were performed on a north-eastwards extension to the Acropolis prospect grid, to map the inferred extent of dense basement rocks east of drillhole ACD6. Diamond drillhole ASD2 was completed to TD 1148.4 m after reaching basement at 1030 m, which consists of unaltered tuffaceous sediments and mafic volcanic rocks.  During the second quarter of 1984, limited geophysical work was done. Plotting of downhole temperature log data revealed a consistently high thermal gradient associated with the Tregolana Shale, regardless of the nature of underlying units. Modelling of gravity data for the prominent Arcoona structure, based on ties to the density log run in hole ASD2, indicated that the feature is caused by a large basement block having a comparatively small density contrast (as low as 0.06 g/cubic cm). Diamond drillholes WRD14, WRD15 and WRD16 were completed at Wirrda Well. A thin sequence of Pre-Adelaidean Pandurra Formation, strata of which had not previously been recognised in the cover at this particular prospect, was intersected below 443.3 m depth in hole WRD16.  During the third quarter of 1984, modelling and interpretation of gravity data for Oak Dam allowed the selection of a drill site on the eastern margin of the gravity high with a source earlier identified in hole AD4 as being a haematitic sediment sequence. Diamond drillhole ACD12 was completed to TD 1001.7 m at Acropolis, on the south-eastern flank of the prospect, and was geophysically logged with the now customary suite of wireline gamma ray/resistivity/phase IP tools.  During the fourth quarter of 1984, diamond drillhole AD7 was completed at TD 954.6 m, after reaching basement at 876.5 m depth. The basement consists of 20 m of strongly haematitic oxidised felsic volcanic rocks overlying sericitised granite identical to that encountered in hole AD3, i.e. cut by pervasive fine-grained sericite dykes. No mineralisation was seen, and assay values were uniformly low except for slightly elevated uranium levels in the ferruginous conglomerate at the pre-Pandurra Formation unconformity, expressed as a 1500 counts per second spike in the gamma ray log. Diamond drillhole OFD2 located near White Dam was completed at TD 475 m to investigate a low amplitude magnetic high in an area of tectonic interest situated just south of the Andamooka Precious Stones Field. Basement in the form of fresh granite was entered at 380 m, which is cut by several medium grained felsic dykes, but shows no other veining or alteration.

abstract: A small licence area covering the extent of precious opal workings around Andamooka township was originally granted to the Stuart Shelf joint venture partners on 11/1/1982 as EL 959, which tenement under the newly amended provisions of the Mining Act conferred on them the rights to explore the subsurface beyond 50 m depth beneath the ground surface for base metals, while protecting the near-surface interests of the miners with opal leases already granted. No work took place for 3 months due to adverse weather conditions, but by April 1982 when a replacement EL 993 was issued, WMC had commenced detailed grid-based ground geophysical surveys to delineate the Bills Lookout West high intensity magnetic and gravity anomalies. This work confirmed the unusual nature of the geophysical target, and plans were made to drill the major magnetic peak located on the northern side of the prospect grid. Multifrequency IP surveys were conducted along three grid lines crossing the magnetic high, but did not indicate the presence of any resistivity or phase anomaly associated with it. Further ground geophysical surveying was carried out over the next six months to complete detailed coverage of the licence area, which assisted WMC with defining a number of magnetic anomalies and variably resistive basement zones, but no significant gravity features were found. Vertical exploratory diamond drillhole OFD1 was drilled during September-October 1982 to test the main magnetic anomaly that is centred just west of Pimba Ridge. The hole was percussion precollared to 206.6 m depth, and then was diamond cored to a total depth of 521.4 m. Basement was reached at 387.05 m depth, and consists of mixed granitoid rocks which are moderately magnetic.

abstract: A dipolar aeromagnetic anomaly seen at Norton Dam was examined by conducting grid-based ground gravity and magnetic surveys. A north-west trending, shallowly buried basic dyke is inferred to occur at this location, intruded within the Pandurra Formation, which here outcrops through younger Mesozoic and Cainozoic cover. The grid area lies just to the west of a prominent north-northwest trending lineament and probable fault downthrown to the east, in a similar structural setting to the Acropolis Dam prospect. The depth to the source of the broad magnetic anomaly was estimated to be of the order of 1100 m. A subjective residual gravity anomaly of less than 0.5 mGal was interpreted from the gravity data, striking north-south and coinciding with the surface projection of the source of the magnetic anomaly. The depth to basement (top of the Gawler Range Volcanics) here is estimated to be about 500 m. A recommendation was made that a single deep drillhole be put down to test the source of the magnetic anomaly, but no action was taken before it was decided to let licence tenure lapse.

abstract: Exploration over the now surrendered ground, which had been successively incorporated within ELs 301, 513 and 769, was initially directed at a search for stratabound base metal deposits which might exist within the flat-lying Neoproterozoic and Mesoproterozoic metasedimentary sequence of the Stuart Shelf. However, the eventual drilling of 23 vertical percussion holes (total penetration 4799 m) and one diamond hole (to TD 320 m) failed to intersect significant mineralisation.  Work performed during the latest licence tenure period has consisted of flying four low level aeromagnetic / radiometric survey traverses across the Norton Dam magnetic / radiometric anomaly, followed by the percussion drilling on this prospect grid of one vertical precollar hole, to 390 m total depth, in preparation for a planned second, deeper diamond drillhole to look for Olympic Dam - style mineralisation. Hole PIL19 remained in Pandurra Formation for its entire length, penetrating the complete sequence of lithologies recognised from drilling elsewhere on the Stuart Shelf. No significant geochemical anomalism was recorded from this drillhole. Variable magnetic susceptibilities read from drill cuttings are attributed to differing amounts of magnetite and ilmenite and heavy mineral laminae in the units, but do not indicate that the source of the magnetic anomaly lies within the Pandurra interval.  Indeed, Seltrust's subsequent geophysical data interpretations have indicated that the estimated depth to crystalline basement here is probably in excess of 1 km, which factor, together with the lack of recognisable coincident gravity / magnetic responses, has served to discourage undertaking any further exploration.

abstract: Over the report period Agip Australia completed the drilling and geophysical logging of 39 open rotary holes totalling 3845 m to investigate if economic coal seams occur within Permian sediments of the southern Arckaringa Basin.  Although the Permian Stuart Range Formation and the Carboniferous Boorthanna Formation were intersected, the target unit, the Permian Mount Toondina Formation, was absent.  Consequently, no further exploration for coal will be carried out. Combined gravity and ground magnetic surveys were conducted in parts of ELs 796 and 799, in an attempt to further delineate anomalies characteristic of Olympic Dam type mineralisation. Magnetic and gravity anomalies were defined over grids laid out at Danae Hill, Billa Kalina and Lake Younghusband and their likely source depths modelled.  The interpreted magnetic source bodies of BIF and amphibolite were not seen by Agip as worthy of drilling for possible uranium.  Stockdale's regional diamond exploration programme of northern Stuart Shelf areas subcropping the Arckaringa Basin on BILLA KALINA and KINGOONYA, conducted after a farm-in to Agip's failed coal and uranium exploration acreage, included an aerial magnetic, radiometric and EM (VLF) survey over EL 799 (Aerodata-McPhar, 1982), reconnaissance heavy mineral sampling using helicopter support, a Landsat lineament and geomorphic study, photointerpretation, stream sediment sampling over areas covered by Bulldog Shale, and re-sampling of AGIP drillholes. Isolated and scattered garnet indicator minerals were recovered from both the Bulldog outcrop and from inliers of older Cadna-owie Formation, but were inferred to have been derived from a secondary source related to primary kimberlite intrusions. title: Spencer Gulf. Progress reports to licence expiry/full surrender, for the period 12/2/1981 to 11/2/83.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Northern Spencer Gulf;Point Lowly;Blanche Harbour;Yatala Harbour;1982 Northern Spencer Gulf Aerial Magnetic Survey
Doc No: Env 04309
abstract: A 900 line km detailed aeromagnetic survey was carried out over the northern extremity of Spencer Gulf, in a search for possible Olympic Dam style mineralisation associated with a significant and complex magnetic high anomaly that is located almost entirely within the gulf. An earlier interpretation of the BMR's regional magnetic data had suggested that the source of this anomaly lay at > 650 m depth below sea level. However, the increased sensitivity of the presently reported heli-borne magnetic survey (60 E-W lines flown at 500 m line spacing, with a nominal 10 m detector height above water, compared with the BMR's 150 m terrain clearance) has resolved the original anomaly into a large number of individual magnetic highs and lows. It is suggested that the whole anomalous area is the result of an uplift of the magnetic bedrock, with its upturned edge sharply terminated under the centre of the gulf by strong downfaulting to the west, which has later been cross-cut by additional faults having a NW-SE strike. Importantly, the likely depth of overburden above the magnetic sources has been revised to be generally less than 300 m, making it comparable with that found at Olympic Dam.

abstract: Exploration as part of a continuing regional search for possible diamondiferous kimberlites was undertaken 70 km west-northwest of Roxby Downs.  Extensive sampling of current drainage lines in interdune swales, plus loam sampling in other geomorphologically exhumed palaeodrainage locations, revealed a broad dispersion pattern of kimberlitic indicator minerals which was interpreted as not reflecting a primary source.  An examination of past drillhole geological data was undertaken to try to determine if the indicator grain dispersions correlated with the predominant sedimentary lithologies, but no strong relationship was evident. title: RB 56/00079 Amdel 00241 Bromine from bitterns.
notes:
Notes: Copy in Env 04486. Amdel project: 1/1/60. Published by SADM in: Mining Review, Adelaide. No. 118 (1965); p:70-77. Envelope includes progress reports 1 to 7. See also RB 00721, RB 00726, RB 00725.
Doc No: RB 56/00079
Amdel 00241
abstract: The South Australian Government Department of Mines accepted a proposal from AMDL to examine the recovery of bromine from bitterns in South Australia. Production of salt from sea water by solar evaporation in this State is approaching 400,000 tons per year. This represents approximately two thirds of the salt in the sea water treated, the remainder being rejected in bitterns. Since the concentration of bromine in the sea is 1/300 of the sodium chloride present, the bromine available in bitterns is 1/200 of the salt production or about 2000 tons annually. During the year 1960/61, imports of bromine compounds into Australia were:  a. Ethylene dibromide containing 900 tons of bromine b. Potassium bromate containing 6 tons of bromine c. Potassium bromide containing 30 tons of bromine d. Sodium compounds containing 25 tons of bromine e. Petrol additives containing 250 tons of bromine  making the total imports of bromine about 1200 tons. There is no local production of bromine or bromine compounds but clearly the potential exists. Since the bulk of the bromine is imported as ethylene dibromide, it may be advantageous to produce this compound directly, rather tahn to recover elemental bromine in a marketable form. The dibromide forms readily by addition of bromine to ethylene. The growth of the petroleum refining industry in Australia may make ethylene available for this purpose - the gas is already being produced in the Altona petrochemical plant near Melbourne. Alternatively ethylene can be produced fairly readily from ethyl alcohol, which is freely available from industrial fermentation plants in several states. In recovery of bromine from bitterns, an oxidant is required. The common reagent for this oxidation is chlorine, which is produced in three states, but not in South Australia. The only alternative oxidant likely to be economical is manganese dioxide, or pyrolusite. There are deposits of this material at pernatty Lagoon, but the low grade has prevented extensive use of the material. If it could be used as an oxidant, the manganese would, at the same time, be dissolved, and recovery of a manganese concentrate should be possible. The initial objectives of the project were therefore twofold:  1. to develop a process for recovery of bromine from bitterns as either elemental bromine or, preferably, as ethylene dibromide, and 2. to examine the use of Pernatty Lagoon manganese ore in the process, and the possibility of manganese recovery.  The conventional process for bromine recovery from brines entails liberation of bromine in the acidified solution by addition of chlorine. The bromine is removed by a current of air at slightly elevated temperatures, and is recovered by condensation, by reaction with scrap iron to give ferrous bromide, or by reaction with sulphur dioxide to give hydrobromic acid. In the latter cases a further chlorine treatment is used to obtain a more concentrated solution from which the bromine can be distilled. Preliminary consideration of reagent costs for these processes showed that, in Australia, the cost of chlorine would be a major portion of the total, and the use of two chlorine treatments should be avoided if possible. Ethylene dibromide is manufactured from ethylene and bromine in a simple reactor. The reaction is exothermic and water cooling of the vessel is required. To combine bromine recovery with ethylene dibromide manufacture, it seems logical to form ethylene dibromide in dilute solution and concentrate this, rather than to produce elemental bromine. Extending this to the limit, ethylene dibromide could be formed in the bittern and recovered by solvent extraction, similar to a scheme which has been proposed elsewhere. Another possibility is to extract the bromine from the bittern with a solvent, which would then serve as a vehicle for ethylene dibromide formation. Finally the bromide could be recovered by distillation. This report describes experimental work and cost estimates aimed at development of a solvent extraction process for recovery of bromine from bitterns as ethylene dibromide.

name: mesac33390
title: Geology of the Cattlegrid mine, [March] 1972 - [December] 1982.
notes:
Geographic Locality: Mount Gunson;Pernatty Lagoon
Doc No: Env 05429 p: 4-129
Drillhole: PDH M250 - M350;N150 - N150;I150 - I350
abstract: This report is intended to be a convenient single reference to the Cattlegrid ore deposit geology. It represents an updated summary of a large amount of data, gleaned largely from internal company reports. The subject matter relates mainly to the geology of the mine pit area, but the report also includes sections on regional setting, deposit evaluation and ore reserves. Exploration research aspects, mill production reports and ore concentrate output shipping summaries are also included. The orebody is a concealed, sandstone-hosted copper (-zinc-lead) sulphide deposit with an economically significant silver content. The stratiform mineralisation is hosted primarily by a localised closely-fractured and brecciated zone developed about the disconformity between the Pandurra Formation and Whyalla Sandstone, and its margins extend upwards and downwards into these units. The breccia zone is considered to be part of a palaeo-weathering profile, of palaeo-permafrost origin. The source of the copper metal is considered to be the pre-Adelaidean volcanic basement. At Cattlegrid, it has been found that copper is the best geochemical indicator, and that IP surveys have proven to be the best geophysical indicator, to buried mineralisation. Within the orebody the assemblage of minerals that has been identified comprises pyrite, marcasite, arseniferous pyrite, carrollite, sphalerite, chalcopyrite, bornite, digenite, djurleite, chalcocite, galena, wittichenite and native bismuth.

abstract: In a search for possible epithermal or sedimentary uranium deposits, plus any base metal mineralisation, in an area located east of Lake Gairdner and approximately 70 km south-west of Woomera, the licensee acquired a 6240 line km airborne magnetic/radiometric survey and later conducted geological mapping and ground follow-up of selected airborne radiometric anomalies, which showed that all of them are related to potassium-rich clays deposited in salt lakes, except for one associated with an outcrop of uraniferous Yardea Dacite. Exploratory percussion drillholes G1 and G2 (total 608 m) tested the mineralisation potential adjacent to a prominent buried fault that had been interpreted from airborne magnetics, whilst elsewhere, hole G3 was drilled to 300 m total depth to address another interpreted magnetic target where there was a probable thin cover of Pandurra Formation and Yardea Dacite over older basement.  All three drillholes failed to encounter significant mineralisation, or to identify any prospective lithologies. Hole G1 penetrated richly magnetite-bearing porphyritic rhyodacite of the Yardea Dacite, carrying chloritic-altered ferromagnesian phenocrysts to 1-2 mm in size.  Minor fluorite, pyrite and calcite were identified in drillhole G2 over the depth interval 156-158 m, in ?Wheepool Rhyolite tuffs and ignimbrites.  Hole G3 was still within massive, un-magnetic Yardea Dacite at total depth.

abstract: Diamond exploration was carried out in an area surrounding the Stuart Creek Opal Field, 30 km north-west of Lake Torrens, to follow up a previously reported discovery of some kimberlitic indicator minerals.  6 out of 20 additional gravel and loam samples taken by CRA were seen to contain kimberlitic indicators. abstract: Exploration was undertaken in two areas 30-40 km north of Port Augusta for possible Olympic Dam type mineralisation emplaced along the Torrens Hinge Zone.  A 4 mGal, barometrically-levelled gravity anomaly previously defined by Western Mining Corp. to the north-west of Baker Dam was tested by a detailed, optically-levelled gravity survey, but no anomaly was found, casting doubt on the original methods used.  However, further reconnaissance gravity surveying identified another, NNW-trending, steep-sided 3 mGal anomaly a few km to the east of Baker Dam, having a possible dense source at 300-500 m depth, but with no coincident magnetic response.  DDH SABD1 was drilled to 803.2 m total depth (302 m percussion pre-collared) at this anomaly location to test a preferred source model of haematitic material occurring within a fault-bounded graben, but none was intersected.  A revised model for the gravity anomaly source, using a combination of slightly thicker Adelaidean units and thicker sequences of Beda Volcanics, is now considered more likely to be correct, but this model has difficulty explaining the anomaly's steep-sided flanks.

abstract: The continuation of copper-gold exploration across the Stuart Shelf region, as part of a newly indentured joint venture project involving Western Mining Corp. (WMC) and British Petroleum (BP), has remained based on the acquisition of detailed ground gravity and magnetic surveys designed to define basement targets for exploratory/stratigraphic percussion and diamond core drilling.  Early in the report period, Geoterrex of Canada were contracted by licence operator WMC to process 22,130 line km of digital data from the company's 1979 Andamooka low-level aeromagnetic/radiometric survey, in order to interpret the locations of faults, geological boundaries and other subsurface features of interest, and to generate automated computer-based estimates of depth to magnetic basement. The final report for this project was supplied to the JV in February 1982.   An experimental deep resistivity sounding survey was conducted during April 1981 at three of WMC's lately drilled prospects, using the newly available Maxi-Probe EMR-16 multifrequency equipment that is under field evaluation by Geoterrex Australia. Effective depth penetration was found to be less than 450 m, with poor resolution of resistivity interfaces from there down to 600 m depth. It was concluded that larger transmit loops, more power and larger transmitter-receiver separations would give the EMR-16 system greater flexibility and depth penetration, allowing it to be more useful for interpreting gravity anomalies on the Stuart Shelf.  During the first quarter of 1981, diamond drillholes were completed at Snake Gully East (SGD2), Island Dam (IDD1), Bopeechee West (BD2) and Oak Dam (AD3). Significant primary copper mineralisation was intersected by drillholes IDD1 and SGD2. In the former, basement rocks entered below 349 m depth consist of sheared and sericite-chlorite altered felsic volcaniclastics overlying pyritic carbonaceous shales. Copper mineralisation is associated with the more strongly chloritised units, e.g. 10 m @ 0.42% Cu from 377-387 m, 17 m @ 0.39% Cu from 403-420 m, and 19 m @ 0.33% Cu from 428-447 m. At Snake Gully, a succession of granites and granite breccias intruded by basic dykes was encountered below 432 m depth, and minor chalcocite, bornite and chalcopyrite are present in the breccia sequence, yielding 4 m @ 0.27% Cu from 490-494 m.  During the second quarter of 1981, diamond drillholes were completed at Saddle Hill (SHD1), Phillips Ridge East (PD3), Arcoona Structure (ASD1), Acropolis (ACD2), Bopeechee (BD1) and Willaroo Lagoon (WLD1). Significant copper mineralisation was intersected by drillhole ACD2 (22 m @ 0.4% Cu from 679-701 m depth, plus 21 m @ 0.51% Cu and 35 ppm U3O8 from 716-737 m) and by the percussion precollar to IDD4 at Island Dam (28 m @ 0.33% Cu from 282-310 m, as bornite and chalcopyrite in sheared felsic volcanic rocks, 800 m west of the intercepts made in IDD1). At BD1, which was deepened from 647 m to a new TD of 941 m, the basement comprises massive arkosic sediments with magnetite and pyrite veining and minor chalcopyrite.  During the third quarter of 1981, diamond drillholes were completed at Acropolis East (ACD3), Bills Lookout East (BLD3), Island Dam (IDD2, IDD3 and IDD4), Oak Dam West (AD4), Snake Gully West (SGD4) and Snake Gully East (SGD5). Significant copper mineralisation was intersected at Acropolis East, at Oak Dam West and at Island Dam. ACD3 reached basement at 640 m depth, and down to TD 1227 m passed through granite breccia with zones of haematite and magnetite-rich matrix containing pyrite and minor chalcopyrite (best assay result 2 m @ 0.3% Cu from 660-662 m, plus 4000 ppm Zn). WMC noted that the basement succession is very similar to granite breccias drilled beneath the main ore zone at Olympic Dam. Uranium values assayed were mostly less than 50 ppm U3O8. At Island Dam, IDD2 penetrated a metasedimentary succession comprising sandstones, siltstone and iron formation, which was unmineralised. This hole was sited on a gravity ridge extending east from the magnetic anomaly on which IDD1 had been drilled early in 1981. IDD3 was drilled 800 m north of IDD1, and encountered granite gneiss between 300 and 567 m depth. IDD4, drilled 800 m west of IDD1 along the strike of the magnetic anomaly, reached basement at 268 m depth and then passed through a succession of strongly altered felsic volcanic rocks and minor siltstones to TD 619 m. Bornite encountered over the depth interval 281-291 m assayed 1.9% Cu and 30 ppm Ag, and is underlain by minor chalcopyrite. AD4 was drilled on a small gravity anomaly flanking the large Arcoona Structure anomaly. Basement was reached at 727 m depth, and down to the hole's TD of 1254 m, it comprised interbedded haematitic siltstone and haematite breccias that appeared to WMC to be very similar to lithologies in the ironstone 'core' block at Olympic Dam. These dense rocks do not contain visible copper mineralisation, but are anomalous in uranium. During this period, WMC carried out a photogrammetrically-controlled regional gravity survey at 1 km station spacing [survey identity and quantum unknown} to infill between previously gridded and detail gravity surveyed areas to the south, west and north of Olympic Dam. No significant gravity anomalies were disclosed by this work. The new data was successfully tied into the surrounding prospect grids' gravity coverage.  During the fourth quarter of 1981, diamond drillholes were completed at Acropolis (ACD4, ACD5), Burden Hill South (BHD1), Burden Hill North (BHD2), Torrens (TD2), Wirrda Well South-east (WRD4) and Wirrda Well (WRD5). Minor copper mineralisation was intersected in BHD2 (0.2% Cu over the depth interval 284.6-297 m, as chalcopyrite, bornite and chalcocite in veins within a metasedimentary succession of gneisses and schists) and in TD2 (sporadic chalcopyrite grading up to 0.29% Cu over 4 m, and 0.19% Zn over 6 m, down to 858 m depth, from within a thick interval of recrystallised magnetite-quartz overlying potash feldspar - rich metasediments). Ground magnetic and gravity surveys were completed in the Todds Dam South area.   Early in 1982, WMC commenced the acquisition of multifrequency induced polarisation (IP) and controlled source audio-magnetotelluric (CSAMT) ground survey measurements on the Stuart Shelf, by obtaining profiles across the Olympic Dam, Wirrda Well and Oak Dam areas. Four profiles at Wirrda Well yielded IP anomalies of resistivity or phase that were deemed worthy of drill testing. Preliminary results available from an IP traverse at Oak Dam suggested that resistivity anomalies are associated with the sulphide-bearing haematite breccias cored in AD1 and with the haematite breccias and siltstones cored in AD4. WMC intends to continue to evaluate electrical survey techniques at prospects where mineralisation is known to occur. During this first quarter of 1982, diamond drillholes were completed at Acropolis (ACD6), Horn Ridge (HRD1), Snake Gully East (SGD6) and Wirrda Well East (WRD6). All of these holes were terminated some distance into various unmineralised basement plutonic or volcanic rocks.  During the second quarter of 1982, diamond drillholes were completed at Torrens (TD3), Horse Well (HWD1), Red Dam (RED1) and Todds Dam South (TOD2W2). HWD1 intersected bornite and minor chalcocite within haematite veined, brecciated felsic volcanics after reaching basement at 861 m depth (best assay 17 m @ 0.64% Cu from the depth interval 902-919 m). This hole was terminated at 1097 m after failing to penetrate any source for the targeted magnetic anomaly. TOD2W2 reached basement at 612 m depth, and was terminated at TD 786 m. Here the upper part of the basement comprises chlorite-altered granite, then passes downwards into a strongly sheared, chlorite and graphite schist zone above aluminous metasediments. A 17 m thick zone within the strongly altered rocks contains abundant magnetite and moderate radioactivity. However, the magnetic rocks are insufficient to explain the magnetic anomaly on which the hole was sited.  During the third quarter of 1982, diamond drillholes were completed at Acropolis (ACD7) and Hunter Hill (HUD1).  Diamond drilling (then incomplete) of WRD9 at Wirrda Well prospect, which is located about 20 km south-southeast of Olympic Dam, encountered significant intercepts of primary copper mineralisation, averaging 0.8% Cu over 215 m in drill core cut below 419 m depth and containing 2-3 m lenses grading up to 3.6 % Cu and 36 ppm Ag, associated with haematite veining developed in altered granite over the depth interval 391-631 m.  Chalcocite was intersected over a 70 m thick above 500 m depth, and minor bornite and chalcopyrite below this depth. In consequence of this discovery, WMC considered that Wirrda Well could represent the best prospect on the Stuart Shelf licence, as it contains large coincident gravity and magnetic anomalies, and recent ground electrical surveys performed there had indicated the existence of a broad, low resistivity polarisable layer extending in a south-eastwards direction from the gravity anomaly centre.  In a press release made on 12/10/1982, the company gave details of the mineralised drill intercepts made at the prospect to date, and said that from the nine drillholes so far put in there, it is known that the mineralisation style has some similarities to that seen at Olympic Dam, although it does not contain recoverable uranium or gold. The overlying cover sequence varies in thickness from 355 m to 436 m. During this reporting period WMC continued with its programme of experimental electrical surveying, by acquiring CSAMT coverage at Wirrda Well, Torrens, Island Dam and Winjabbie prospects, and by beginning to acquire complex resistivity (CR) ground surveys, run initially at Acropolis and at Island Dam using a 600 m dipole-dipole separation. In addition, 1 km x 1 km spaced regional gravity surveying was commenced to investigate the shallow basement area located between the Andamooka Opalfield and the Island Dam prospect grid.  During the fourth quarter of 1982, additional diamond drillholes were completed at Wirrda Well (WRD9, WRD9W1, WRD10 and WRD11) to investigate resistivity anomalies detected within altered granite. At WRD9, where the drillhole had to be wedged off at 667 m depth because of drilling problems, low grade copper mineralised intercepts were made over a broad interval below that depth, with scattered higher grade zones including 5.35 m @ 2.98% Cu, 12 ppm Ag and 150 ppm U3O8 from 668-673.35 m, and 15 m @ 1.75% Cu, 14 ppm Ag and 260 ppm U3O8 from 692-707 m. The mineralisation occurs within haematite-magnetite veins and irregular matrix stringers within chlorite and sericite-altered granite and granite breccia. Only minor low grade copper intercepts were made in WRD10 and WRD11, in similarly moderately altered granite having minor haematite veining. Other drillholes completed in the quarter were put in at Acropolis (ACD9) and Murdie prospects (MRD1). The latter hole, located on Lake Torrens, was completed at TD 918 m after penetrating at 806 m a basement consisting of massive to weakly banded volcanic beds (possible tuffs). Intense magnetite veining and alteration logged over the depth interval 833-884 m was thought to contribute to the magnetic anomaly on which this hole was sited. No significant mineralisation was encountered. WMC commenced downhole wireline geophysical logging of its still accessible deep exploratory drillholes during this period, running electrical logs in holes WRD9, WRD10, WRD11, ACD8 and ACD9. The three lines of CR survey data recently obtained from Acropolis yielded no anomalies of interest, and common instances of electromagnetic coupling caused doubtful interpretation results for both resistivity and AMT spectra. However, it was believed by WMC that the less ambiguous resistivity anomalies that had been detected at other nearby prospects such as Island Dam and Oak Dam might in part reflect real variations in the conductivity of the cover sequence, as well as the effects of thickness changes of units within the Pandurra Formation. On the JV's newly granted EL 993 covering the Andamooka Opalfield, 55 line km of ground magnetic profiles and 21 line km of gravity traverses were acquired at the end of 1982.
